speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important and urgent matter.
Because the present imbroglio about jurisdiction over telecommunications threatens to lead to conflicts, the consequences of which could be serious for the country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the government immediately order that a federal-provincial conference be held on the constitution for the purpose of sharing definitively provincial and federal jurisdiction over telecommunications.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the collateral matters being revealed during the course of Chief Justice Estey's inquiry into the financial affairs of Air Canada and the increasing evidence that the top executives of our national air carrier are either unable or unwilling to follow the enabling statutory guidelines which set out Air Canada's specific authorization and terms of reference for doing business as a Crown corporation authorized by this Parliament, the latest such instance, Mr. Speaker, being a confidential agreement with the Tourism Minister of Lebanon for the promotion of Air Canada in that country, a matter which has diplomatic overtones, the unusual nature of which is well illustrated by the quote from John McGill, Vice-President of Air Canada, who allegedly said: "I don't understand the mores and morals of the Middle East"-obviously, Mr. Speaker, it is not only the Middle East that the executives of Air Canada do not understand-I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That this House instruct the Minister of Transport, entirely apart from the report of Chief Justice Estey which will be tabled in due course, that there is now sufficient evidence that the minister make immediate changes at the top level executive structure of Air Canada to assure that management conducts the airline's affairs in a way that will be businesslike, and within the statutory authority granted by Parliament and in accordance with accepted international procedures, so that Air Canada may be a credit to Canada in every respect.

Mr. Speaker, the confusion will occur only in the minds of those lacking intelligence to distinguish between two distinct coins. subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members know that the first part of the Foreign Investment Review Act, governing takeovers of Canadian business enterprises, was proclaimed into force on April 9, 1974. When the bill was before parliament I undertook, on behalf of the government, that the second part of the act, phase II, relating to the establishment of new foreign-controlled businesses in Canada, would not come into force until the government was satisfied on two scores.
The first was that the government should have gained some experience in the actual administration of the review process under phase I. We have now had well over a year's experience and we are satisfied that the review process is working well.
The other commitment was that phase II would not be introduced until there had been further consultations with the provincial governments. During the past year there have been several meetings with representatives of all provincial governments. Those meetings have involved very full discussions on the administrative procedures for consultation on individual cases between the federal and provincial authorities, and I am pleased to say that there is general agreement that the procedures which have evolved are sound and workmanlike.
Accordingly, the government has now, by proclamation, fixed the date on which phase II is to come into force. That date is October 15 of this year. The lead time we have

provided will give investors and their advisers the necessary opportunity to become familiar with the phase II guidelines and regulations. It is also intended to avoid disruption in investment plans which are now being developed.
It should be noted in this regard that investments which are under way on October 15 are not reviewable under the act to the extent that they are established businesses. To show that a business was already established by October 15 it will not be necessary to show that the business was fully operational on that date. Where there are one or more employees, together with contractual obligations or other definite commitments relating to the new business, those factors should be enough to show that the new business has been established and is therefore not subject to review.
In the administration of phase II of the act we will, of course, continue to follow the procedures that have been developed for close consultation on individual cases with the provincial governments. We will also ensure that there is effective co-ordination between the Foreign Investment Review Agency and other departments and agencies of the federal government.
In this regard I would like to advise investors who intend to apply for incentives under the Regional Development Incentives Act, and whose investment proposals are also subject to review under the Foreign Investment Review Act, that they should discuss their plans first with the appropriate provincial or regional office of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I want to assure hon. members that there will be no unnecessary delay in investment programs important to the development of designated regions of the country through duplication of administrative procedures.
I should again like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of the Foreign Investment Review Act is not to block foreign investment from any source or to discourage it but, rather, to ensure that such investment is of significant benefit to Canada. Since its beginnings Canada has had to rely heavily on foreign investment to help us develop this country. Clearly, it has been beneficial. We shall continue to need a great deal more investment in Canada by our friends abroad if we are to develop our full potential as this government is determined to do.
A mere glance at the guidelines concerning related business will clearly indicate that great care has been exercised to ensure that there will be no interference with investment for the maintenance and expansion of the ongoing business in Canada. This was clearly parliament's intention when the act was passed into law.
Mr. Speaker, the House is aware that ownership and control of enterprises engaged in the extraction and processing of uranium are matters of important concern to the national interest and to Canadians generally. The government's intention to limit nonresident ownership in this industry is well known. The government is considering alternative measures to consolidate this policy with respect to the ownership of uranium mines within the general ambit of our policy regarding foreign ownership and control of the Canadian economy.
July 18, 1975

Mr. Speaker, I am also tabling, on behalf of the government, copies in both official languages of new "Principles of International Business Conduct." These are not to be confused with the guidelines concerning related business under the Foreign Investment Review Act. They are intended as an updating and a replacement of "Guiding Principles of Good Corporate Behaviour in Canada" which were announced by the late Hon. Robert Winters on March 31, 1966. Like the earlier set of guiding principles of good corporate behaviour, the new set of principles reflects broad government policy regarding the activities and responsibilities of foreign-controlled business enterprises in Canada. They thus provide an added indication of the sort of benefits the government looks for in assessing investment proposals under the Foreign Investment Review Act. But they are directed towards all foreign-controlled enterprises doing business in Canada, whether or not they are involved with the Foreign Investment Review Act.
The basic content of the 1966 guiding principles has been retained. However, we have to recognize that new developments have taken place and that these developments should be reflected in the revised principles. In 1966, the government was especially concerned over certain financial aspects of the activities of foreign subsidiaries in Canada because of particular balance of payments measures which were introduced at that time by the United States. The guiding principles did not lay particular stress on the need for subsidiary companies to have more autonomy or sufficiently underline the need to identify more closely with Canada economically, socially, and culturally.
A major omission from the old principles of good corporate behaviour was that they made no reference to the conditions under which foreign or foreign-controlled technology and know-how may be transferred to a Canadian subsidiary. These can often serve to inhibit the local subsidiary from operating at its full potential. To emphasize our interest in the technology-related activities of foreign-owned subsidiaries, we have added a new principle, number 14, and we have tied it in with the observance of the preceding principles.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for providing us with a copy of his statement a few hours ago. The opposition endorses the principle of less foreign ownership in the Canadian economy and agrees that quick action is necessary to monitor the amount of foreign investment we have in the Canadian economy, but we wonder why the government and the minister are making an announcement at this particular time of the proclamation of phase II.
We have been told that the minister had to wait until he had reached some agreement with the provinces on the operation of phase II, and until he knew whether phase I was working and how it was working, before he was prepared to go ahead with this new proclamation. On the latter score, that is whether phase I is working, I am not surprised that there has been a delay, because it was not until more than a year after the proclamation of phase I that the foreign investor, the Canadian public and members of this House had any indication of the specific criteria to be applied in the evaluation of proposed foreign
Foreign Investment Review Act investment. It would have been preferable had the agency become familiar with these criteria somewhat sooner.
On the first point, that of provincial consultation, I wonder whether the minister is prepared to assure the House that his consultations with the provinces had greater scope than making them aware of what he intended to do. I hope the minister will take the time to assure the House in more definite terms that all the provinces across Canada agree with the imminent proclamation of phase II.
I am sure the minister was faced with a difficult balancing act in deciding on the proclamation of phase I in October. The need for proclamation is there, but the full act comes into force at a time when Canada is suffering from recession and is plagued with one of the most significant balance of payments problems it has ever had. After listening to the minister, I conclude that he is quite satisfied that the critically needed foreign capital inflows will not be disrupted by the proclamation of phase II, and that phase II will not damage the business confidence required for the large volume of equally critically required new capital investment.
I hope the minister will also find the time, perhaps today at the conclusion of the remarks of the various spokesmen on this issue, to indicate more fully that he has had discussions with his colleagues, with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in particular, and that there is no concern about the implementation of the proclamation of phase II at this time with respect to our serious balance of payments problems.
Although I have not had the opportunity to study the guidelines concerning related business in detail, I find at this stage that they are relatively non-controversial, although there are one or two peculiarities. For instance, vertical integration is classified as related business expansion under guidelines 1 and 2. Thus, we find the government again doing what they do so often, taking action on the one hand which is contravened by action on the other, because we see that they will now apply vertical integration through the Foreign Investment Review Act, while they created a royal commission on corporate power to study this problem to find out whether it is a good thing for the Canadian economy. Guidelines 4 and 5 also seem to be in some disagreement. Guideline 4 permits expansion if the same technology is used, and guideline 5 only if the technology is new and Canadian.
We are also pleased to see some comment in the report about the policy with respect to ownership of uranium. However, we hope the government does not believe that by looking at this ownership issue they have, in fact, solved the problem or indeed put forward a solution that is adequate for all Canadians as to how we are going to deal with the export of this most important product.
The minister has also provided us with an expanded set of criteria under which the significant benefit test is to be conducted. We can only say we hope the minister has made up his mind clearly and distinctly about this matter, because the hallmark and characteristic feature of the present government is to do something one day and change it the next. If we are to have the sort of investment we need in this country, the business community must have confidence that the government knows precisely what they will do.

Much of the need for this legislation would be reduced if the government were only to take a more positive attitude toward business in this country. Foreign ownership regulations are really only a short-term answer to the over-all problem of foreign investment and the development of the Canadian economy. The real answer to our problems lies in the generation of a healthy Canadian business climate, and the minister must know that his job is not complete until he has measures installed which will accomplish this end and until he has produced what Canadians have been looking for for a very long time, namely, some sort of industrial strategy to guide the development of the Canadian economy.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Foreign Investment Review Act was debated in the House, the NDP supported it because it represented an improvement over the then existing situation with respect to foreign investment, that is to say, over a situation in which there were no controls in this major area. We reserved judgment on the act, however, as it was clear from the way in which it was worded that the attitude of the government to foreign investment and the regulations implementing the act would be the crucial determinants on the issue. We now know, if there were any doubts before, that the government had no real intention of limiting or controlling foreign investment in Canada.
Our support of the Foreign Investment Review Act was on the basis that it would encourage rational control of investment in the Canadian economy so that Canadian resources would be developed in such a way that the maximum benefit would go to the people of Canada as a whole and not to foreign-owned, multinational corporations. The prime benefit had to remain here, and not abroad. However, as the operation of the first phase of the act demonstrated beyond doubt, this was not the purpose the government had in mind for its own bill. Its purpose was simply to stem the criticism of Canadians legitimately concerned that the Canadian economy was being more and more controlled by outside governments and outside corporations. There is no discernible pattern in the agency's activity since the passage of the bill in relation to takeover approvals, which have run at the rate of some 80 per cent of all applications.
The guidelines for takeover are so vague as to be worthless. The reason for this is that the government does not intend to plan in a rational way investment patterns in Canada. Every time this government gets into trouble, under any circumstances, in the economy it runs off and asks foreign companies to bail it out: witness recent speeches-and by "recent" I mean in the last six months- by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), both at home and abroad, assuring foreign investors that they would have no problem at all in embarking upon ventures in the Canadian economy. Hence the expressed reason for the delays in proclaiming part II of the act.
The regulations under part II clearly demonstrate that the government's real position will not be found in the royal commission set up by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to investigate corporate power, which is a sham if

ever there was one created in Canadian politics. The real attitude toward the power of corporations in Canada, and particularly multinational corporations, is to be found in what is included in the regulations just tabled by the minister and, more importantly, to be found in what is not included in those regulations.
The statement of the minister is a blatant and shocking attempt to reassure foreign investors that the government has no serious intention of interfering in the slightest in their investment decisions. I wish to quote briefly from the minister's statement as follows: "I should again like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of the Foreign Investment Review Act is not to block foreign investment from any source or to discourage it but, rather, to ensure that such investment is of significant benefit to Canada. Since its beginnings Canada has had to rely heavily on foreign investment to help us develop this country. Clearly, it has been beneficial."
Later the minister said: "A mere glance at the guidelines concerning related business will clearly indicate that great care has been exercised to ensure that there will be no interference with investment for the maintenance and expansion of ongoing business activities in Canada." That sentence in particular is one of the understatements of the century in Canadian politics, and one of the great understatements of the underlying economic philosophy of the Liberal Party.
Under the regulations, the list of exclusions of new foreign-owned businesses which do not need government approval to start operating is exhaustive: it is difficult to imagine any foreign investor who would have to apply for approval before establishing a new business. But of even greater importance is what this second phase does not review, the vertical integration of multinational corporations. The list of exclusions encourages the future development of vertical integration in our economy. What are the problems associated with it? Let me list the problems for the Canadian economy and, therefore, for the people of Canada, with further vertical integration. First, such integration allows transfer pricing between related companies which can artificially increase prices in Canada. Second, it reduces tax liabilities and encourages tax dodges at home and abroad. Third, it continues the trend to have research and development done outside Canada, making us increasingly technologically dependent on other countries but particularly on the United States. Fourth, it encourages the importing of machinery from foreign-based multinationals with plants in Canada. Fifth, it discourages the export of machinery and technology which would compete with the American parent company.
The exclusion of any concern over vertical integration means, to the New Democratic Party that the government has bypassed the most important aspect of the foreign domination of our economy. This is presumably a summary of the position that will be taken by this Liberal government until the next election, when it will probably trot out some other vague, unspecified and general commitment to deal with the problem of foreign ownership. But I hope that finally the poeple of Canada will shed whatever illusions they may have about the determination of this government to do anything about regaining economic independence for Canada. subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his statement the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) mentioned that he was pleased with the good feeling and understanding which existed during his consultations with the provincial governments. We were thus spared the disgraceful scenes which occurred during the last weeks between the federal Minister of Communications and his provincial counterparts, especially the Quebec minister. However, I think that the interests were not the same. In the communication field, domestic interests are involved while the interests which concern the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in foreign investments are especially foreign interests of multinational companies which are much greater. It is then easier to agree on such matters.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I was struck by points in the minister's statement, particularly when he assures foreign investors that their applications for regional development grants would be considered and processed rapidly. The minister wants to assure hon. members that there will be no undue delay in the investment program necessary to the development of designated areas in Canada because of red tape duplication.
We know how slow the department or officials of the Department of regional Economic Expansion are in considering or accepting applications for grants from Canadian companies or businesses. I remember a case when a contractor or businessman applied for a $40,000 grant. It is not all that much. All possible complications were made to delay the awarding of the grant probably to discourage that businessman. We are a lot nicer to foreign investors than we are to Canadians who want to create new jobs and offer people the consumer goods they are asking for.
We know how things go generally regional development grants awarded to foreign companies who come to invest in this country amount to about 35 per cent. And those foreign investors get another 55 per cent from the local market so they have to come up with only 10 per cent of their own money in Canadian investments. That prompts us to say that somehow they are being paid to put us out. We know that about 80 per cent at least of our industries, and particularly those which are most important and profitable, are in the hands of foreigners.
Mr. Speaker, rather than say we are happy to promote foreign investments in Canada we should strive instead to encourage Canadians to own our own industries and businesses so we will know better what Canadian consumers want. I think one is best served by himself. That is what I wanted to say, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the minister tell the House whether he has any impression that the proclamation will have any serious positive or negative effect on the Canadian balance of payments situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it will have any significant effect on the balance of payments question. Let me put it in this context: we are faced with a deficit in our current account this year of probably between $4 billion and $5 billion; perhaps closer to $5 billion. Foreign investors do not invest in Canada, or anywhere else, because we are running a deficit in our balance of payments account; they invest because they see industrial opportunities. That will be the basis in the future, as it has been in the past. When foreign investments are made, they will not be motivated, in other words, by a desire to help Canada finance any deficit in its current account.
The second point that I should like to make is that all deficits in the past that I am aware of have relied far more heavily, in terms of the financing of the current account deficit, on portfolio investments, that is to say, debt, borrowings of municipalities and provinces, institutions and corporations in foreign markets. I would expect that

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister why he is excluding the vertical integration of multinationals from the screening under the act. It seems to me this is the biggest area of foreign enterprise. When we were dealing with the act in committee about two years ago, we tried to nail the minister down on this question of the regulations and he refused to make any commitment on it. Take, for example, a foreign-owned food company: would it be allowed to establish a farm machinery company and not be screened for doing so, and then in turn be able to supply the food to retail or wholesale outlets? Are there any regulations when it comes to vertical integration and, if not, why not? This seems to me to be a major loophole in the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the regulations to the attention of the hon. member in relation to the particular example he used of a food company going into the tractor business. If he were to read the regulations he would find such a company would not meet the conditions of relatedness. That kind of an arrangement, in my view, would in all likelihood be seen as an unrelated activity and therefore screenable.
As an example, we could use the constituency of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). There we have a very large automobile manufacturer, General Motors. A few years ago that company decided to build a battery plant. That is a form of vertical integration. I do not know whether the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby is against that kind of investment. It seems to me, in the nature of things, that anybody in the automobile manufacturing business is likely to be more efficient if they can integrate back. I think the constituency of Oshawa-Whit-by is a good example of that process at work.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PHASE II OF LEGISLATION

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it took longer than I would have wished-and I have stated that on other occasions- for one reason: it was a consultative arrangement. As the hon. member may remember, the provinces sent me a telex at the end of the year, asking for further consultations. We had a series of consultations with officials of the provinces, including Manitoba. I do not think it would have been right to introduce the second proclamation without having completed that consultation process to the full satisfaction of the provinces concerned.

speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ABOLISH DEATH PENALTY AND INCREASE MANDATORY TERM OF IMPRISONMENT FOR MURDER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, very briefly, the purpose of this bill to amend the Criminal Code is to abolish, once and for all, the death penalty, the taking of human life by society. At the same time, however, these amendments are intended at last to provide the Canadian public with some real assurance of safety and security by dramatically increasing the mandatory term of imprisonment, without parole consideration, to 25 years for a much broadened category of murder. My colleague for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) and I also believe that these proposals will provide criminal elements with the kind of deterrent they will understand.

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES PRODUCTION SHARING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
1.	Is there any dollar amount affixed to procurement under the production sharing agreements between the Department of National Defence and its US counterpart?
2.	How involved is the economic and inter-governmental process with requirements of military procurements?
3.	How critical is the balance of payments impact of defence procurements?
4.	How is the procurement effort guided in terms of appreciation for the present and future potentials of the economy in fields of research, development and technology of military requirements?
5.	To what general need is the defence procurement mechanism appropriate for Canada?
6.	To what extent is there Canadian direction and control of the major military systems procured by the Department of Supply and Services?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES PRODUCTION SHARING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Industry, Trade and
Order Paper Questions
Commerce, National Defence, and Supply and Services as follows: 1. Canada/United States Production Sharing Arrangements were originally worked out in 1959 by the Canadian Department of Defence Production and the United States Department of Defense. Responsibility for the Canadian side of these arrangements was transferred in 1968 to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. There is no dollar amount affixed to procurement under the Production Sharing Arrangements but the long term goal is to achieve a rough balance in reciprocal defence procurement.
2.	As part of the equipment acquisition process, much inter-governmental and inter-departmental discussion takes place to ensure that the most cost effective and economically attractive arrangement is arrived at consistent with meeting the military requirements. The Department of Supply and Services is responsible, as far as it is economically practicable to do so, for maintaining a Canadian production base adequate to supply the material requirements of the Department of National Defence. Cooperative supply arrangements, through NATO or other intergovernmental arrangements have helped to lessen the cost of developing and providing complex or unique equipment.
3.	In relation to the overall value of transactions entering into the Canadian balance of payments calculations, the value of defence procurement transactions is minimal (estimated to be less than Vi of 1 per cent). The value of such transactions, however, is one factor considered in the selection and acquisition process.
4.	Technical specialists in the Department of National Defence and the Department of Supply and Services maintain close contact with all Canadian centres of research and development in industry, government and the universities to ensure we are fully informed of all developments which could meet military applications. Similarly effort is directed where possible and practical to concentrate on fields of technology and products which offer the broadest commercial, and therefore employment benefits to Canadian industry: for example, advanced communications systems, and new aircraft engine designs.
5.	As long as Canada has defence forces, there will be a need to procure equipment to support these forces. The defence procurement mechanism is appropriate for Canada in as much as it strives to: (a) Procure in Canada these items which are technically and economically feasible to produce, (b) Take advantage of defence equipment developments in other countries, and where such equipment meets DND requirements, procure abroad, thereby, reducing costs to DND by eliminating costly development.
(c)	Cooperate with our allies in programs of mutual interest in an attempt to eliminate costly duplication of effort and take advantage of economics of scale in production.
(d)	Offset defence procurement from abroad, in so far as practicable by promoting the export sale of defence equipment produced in Canada. Canada has developed expertise in the development and production of defence equipment in certain specialized high technology areas such as transport aircraft, aircraft engines and parts, navigation and communication equipment, flight simulators, sonar equipment as well as sub-assemblies and components. Procurement of such equipment in Canada for export assists

July 18, 1975
Order Paper Questions
in maintaining the defence industrial base, as well as assisting manufacturers to penetrate civil markets with products whose manufacture utilizes the expertise and technology acquired in the production of defence equipment.
6.	While Canada may, from time to time, select for technical and economic reasons military equipment and systems which have been designed abroad such systems once acquired are under Canadian direction and control.

speechtext: I am pleased to observe members on the government side intervening. I have listened to some of their contributions and read others. speechtext: I do not intend to deal, basically, with the substance of the excise tax. That subject has been dealt with by other hon. members. It has already been demonstrated beyond doubt that this is a wicked, iniquitous measure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Nor will I associate myself with the completely false suggestion made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that this measure involves certain elements of energy conservation. That is one of the most stupid, one of the most ridiculous arguments I have ever heard advanced in this House-and I am not forgetting the many demonstrations of stupidity and ignorance from time to time on the part of the front benches opposite. I wish to direct the attention of the House to one phase of this bill which has been neglected. Hopefully, I can do this before one o'clock. I refer to the matter of exemptions and the question of who should receive rebates.

July 18, 1975
Excise Tax Act
A cursory examination of what has happened with regard to this measure shows the improvisation, the hasty, ill-conceived, badly prepared and poorly digested nature of this bill which the Minister of Finance took to cabinet with the paste still dripping off it. It was a scissors-and-paste job if there ever was one. I formed those views on examination of the ways and means motion purely for the purposes of comparison. I dealt with this partly the other day in argument to Mr. Speaker. Paragraph 3 of the ways and means motion, (a) to (g) inclusive, lists seven areas where there should be exemptions. I ask hon. members of this House to observe the classes of people who are entitled to apply for and receive exemptions and rebates.
When we examine the original bill, not the reprint ordered by Mr. Speaker, clause 5(4) on page 3, in describing the categories and classes of people and corporations entitled to a rebate refers to paragraphs (a) to (j). In other words, when this bill came before cabinet, in addition to those classes that appear in the ways and means motion there were four other classes which the minister had recommended to cabinet as being available for rebate from the payment of the tax and had included them in the bill. This is quite plain, because clause 5 dealing with the amendment to section 47.1 of the Excise Tax Act has paragraphs (a) to (f). Paragraph (f) is the one which Mr. Speaker ordered to be thrown out. This leaves only five groups.
I point this out simply to establish that the people and corporations suggested as being entitled to a rebate were included so hastily that when the bill came before cabinet there was that degree of uncertainty about it. Cabinet or a cabinet committee obviously changed it materially, throwing out four of the categories and substituting the one which was included in the original bill, namely, those people and corporations covered by section 149 of the Income Tax Act.
I wish to take one minute to show the absolute absurdity of suggesting that those classes enumerated under section 149 of the Income Tax Act be covered. I will read very briefly from the headings in that particular section:
-a municipality in Canada-
That is fine. It was set out in the original ways and means motion and, of course, was carried forward by this section of the Income Tax Act.
-an agricultural organization, a board of trade or a chamber of commerce... a charitable organization ... a corporation that was constituted exclusively for charitable purposes ... a trust all the property of which is held absolutely in trust... the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, incorporated by chapter 75 of the Statutes of Canada... a corporation that was constituted exclusively for the purpose of providing low-cost housing accommodation ... a corporation that was constituted exclusively for the purpose of carrying on or promoting scientific research ... a labour organization or society or a benevolent or fraternal benefit society or order... a mutual insurance corporation ... a limited-dividend housing corporation ... a trust or corporation established or incorporated solely in connection with, or for the administration of, a registered pension fund or plan-
It goes on ad nauseam. I suggest that at the time the hasty insertion was made in cabinet of this particular clause from the Income Tax Act in place of those clauses which the cabinet had thrown out, absolutely no thought

was given to this most important matter of who should be entitled to receive rebates of this tax.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
This goes to the root of the matter. This is a tax of several hundred million dollars. Several classes of people should be entitled to receive rebates of the payment of that tax. Surely, when the Minister of Finance comes to this House he should have something better prepared than he had with regard to this particular question. It was a contempt of this House of Commons for the minister to come here with a bill in the form it was, asking this House to approve it. The bill should not have been brought into this House unless and until the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) had put together a properly conceived program for those people entitled to rebates and the method to be adopted for paying them. Anything else should not be acceptable to this House and is not acceptable to this party.
In conclusion, I say to those who are attempting to blackmail and shove this bill forward by saying that no rebates can be paid, that that is not the case. Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act shows that there is now in place in the Statutes of Canada a method by which rebates can be made without this legislation being passed. I do not suggest the use of that particular procedure any more frequently than need be. However, when we are being blackmailed and told we must pass this bill promptly because there is no way in which people can get rebates, I say that is not so; I give the lie to those who make that assertion and say there is a method by which it can be done.

Mr. Speaker, in introducing the excise tax of ten cents a gallon for private automobile use of gasoline, the government has clearly indicated its failure to develop a comprehensive energy policy or even outline the bare bones of what might take place in the future. It is a tax which it will be difficult to impose fairly; it is a tax which is almost impossible to apply without "working a fiddle", as the saying goes; it is a tax which is so unfair that it does not include all those who travel, and at the same time does not allow the inclusion of those who have no alternative form of travel such as rapid transit. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, if it is a tax designed to serve in the conservation of the environment, then it should apply to airplane travel as well as to the automobile.
Canada shares, along with Australia, the distinction of being the only industrialized country to increase its consumption of petroleum products last year. In the United States, the use of petroleum products dropped in 1974 by
July 18, 1975

4.5	per cent over 1973. This was at a time when we were reducing exports to the United States to conserve our own dwindling supplies and, to make matters much worse, when we were faced with a massive balance of payments deficit of upward of $6 billion, imports of petroleum making up a good percentage of this deficit. The use of petroleum products in the United States is currently being reduced but our use of petroleum products is increasing particularly in areas which are dependent upon offshore supplies.
In Canada there was an over-all rise of 1 per cent, with gasoline consumption rising by 2.8 per cent and gas diesel oil by 4.1 per cent. The consumption of fuel oil dropped by
8.6	per cent, which may well have reflected the mild winter or an effort at conservation on the part of individuals. The decline in the United States was the first in 32 years and it is said to result from the combined effects of product scarcity induced by the Arab embargo, warm weather in the early months, energy conservation efforts, higher product prices and a slowdown in the economy. Most of these factors apply to Canada, but prices were not so high and there was no lead toward conservation.
Today we received the announcement of the second phase of the foreign investment review legislation whose effect will be to further increase our balance of payments problems by discouraging investment in this country. There may well be good reason there should be selective investment in this country, but we do need to remember that we have a balance of payments deficit of $6 billion this year and it is forecast confidently that it will amount to at least $4.7 billion in 1976. Analysis of these figures suggests that Canadians are more aware of the need for conservation of our limited natural resources than are our governments. The crucial shortage in Canada in the energy field is leadership, both by the federal government and by other governments.
Mr. Speaker, this tax is directly brought about by the decline of exports to the United States, with resulting lessening of the yield of the tax to offset the cost of increased imports for Quebec and the maritime provinces. In effect, the government is charging the motoring public world prices for oil which amounts to 25 per cent or so of our total usage. But none of this tax will go to the producing provinces and none will go to the industry to find new sources of gas and oil. Indeed, the yield of this tax may well be used to fund Petro-Can by which the government intends to further intrude upon provincial rights and further intrude on the private oil industry. The minister could well have found enough money merely by withdrawing the activities of Petro-Can and Information Canada; by this means he would have found enough money to pay for the subsidy to eastern consumers.
Nevertheless, if there is any merit in this tax it would be that it signals a retreat from the position that there can be for any length of time a two-price system for oil and gas in Canada much below the world price, or at least the North American price. The use of the two-price system, particularly for diminishing resources like oil and gas, only encourages wasteful use, and industry becomes uneconomic. When finally it is exposed to world trading, it feels the blows; there is diminished activity in exploration and a
Excise Tax Act
lessening of the drive to find alternative sources of energy or to use those alternative sources.
The Science Council of Canada pointed out that we use the equivalent of 55 per cent of oil in energy, making us the second highest per capita users in the world. The factors listed as responsible for this high demand are our climate, our sparse population, a historically low price for energy, and our high standard of living extending to a proliferation of gadgets and benefits.
By resorting to this tax, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) can only further antagonize the producing provinces as well as the consuming provinces. The producing provinces in the west might well complain that their diminishing resources are being sold at lower than competitive prices for which they will receive nothing in return. The producing provinces rightfully have a grievance here, even if they have been too greedy in their demands on the new value of oil. Alberta decided to take two-thirds of the new value of oil and gas, while Saskatchewan and British Columbia decided they should get almost all, with little or nothing for the producers.
The federal government's decision that Canadians should be insulated from much of the increase in OPEC costs was to hold western oil at a level of $6.50 per barrel. In November of 1974, the federal government put into effect a drastic move proposed in May of that year. It disallowed as an expense to oil, gas and other mineral producers every penny of the stiff royalties and other collections being taken by the provinces. The double-taxation measure levies income tax on resource companies in respect of money they do not receive. It drains away a sizeable part of the cash flow left to Alberta producers and leaves Saskatchewan and B.C. in an even worse position than before the OPEC price boost.
Alberta has made some move toward continuing exploration and development, but Saskatchewan and British Columbia have made only minor concessions. Ottawa is now in a spot of its own making. The export tax revenue has been sharply reduced as the government has overpriced Alberta and Saskatchewan oil in the United States market while restricting western production to the current 500,000 barrels a day, the low capacity in order to stretch out reserves for future eastern Canadian needs, and the Minister of Finance now has to charge ten cents a gallon to all the motoring public to maintain his eastern subsidy. All these manipulations by the federal and provincial governments-and the November budget was one of the worst factors-have meant reduced capital for exploration and development.
The increase in the field price of $1.50 per barrel, in the absence of some important changes in producer provinces and federal policies, simply adds to government revenues and leaves little for the industry. It is estimated that royalties and tax in the Alberta production would absorb 75 per cent of any price increase, and Saskatchewan and B.C. production would actually result in governments taking more than 100 per cent.
The recent budget changes of the Minister of Finance will not materially affect the incentive to producers to continue exploration. The Canadian petroleum industry now faces a jungle of rules and regulations, incentives and rebates. It is becoming the most complex system in the

July 18, 1975
Excise Tax Act
world with its mish-mash of federal and provincial schemes. The $1.50 increase per barrel was estimated to return to the industry anything from zero to 40 cents, depending on how you figured it.
The plight of our oil industry can be summed up in a letter written to the shareholders of Madison Oils Limited by its president. Madison Oils is a small Canadian oil company, 99 per cent owned by Canadians, in which all governments have said they are interested. The president said:
The year 1974 will be remembered by all involved in the Canadian oil industry as the year in which the industry got caught in the midst of the dispute between the provincial governments of the oil producing provinces and the dominion government... a dispute in which both parties appear to have completely lost sight of the fact that in order to survive the industry must be allowed a return on investment commensurate with the risks taken.
Governments have abandoned long-standing approaches to taxing the industry and in their haste to grab the profits have also imposed double taxation on the industry. In Madison's case the production from two properties in Saskatchewan produced 5,124 barrels of oil during the period 1st January, 1974, and 30 April, 1975. This sold for a total of $30,970. Madison paid operating costs of $5,860 and royalties and other payments to the Saskatchewan government totalling $13,400-leaving the company with a mere $11,710-38 per cent of the gross. On top of this, since the oil is exported, the dominion government, via the "export tax" shaved off about $5 per barrel, taking a total of almost $26,000 and raising the price to the buyer to a total of approximately $57,000 on which basis Madison's share amounted to just over 20 per cent. Owing to the new double taxation rules the payments to the Saskatchewan government, lost to the company, are considered taxable income ... so that for income tax purposes Madison is subject to tax on $11,710 plus $13,710; taxed at 45 per cent the payment due is $11,300- which were Madison in a taxable position (due to past losses we are not)-would leave Madison with $410 and the dominion government with $37,300. Had pre-1974 patterns continued we would, on the same oil, sold at the same price to the buyer, have been subject to royalty at 1214 per cent or so with the following result... total return, $57,000, operating costs, $5,860, royalty $7,125-leaving Madison with $44,815- instead of the pre-tax return of $11,710 which we received-a difference of $32,000 which would have permitted us to drill and complete one well somewhere, with the possibility of a discovery bringing us new income.
I think that sums up what this government has done to the oil industry. In the report of the Energy Board on Canadian natural gas supply and requirements recently tabled in the House, the board, which is a government appointed group, had this to say at page 84:
-a lack of adequate growth in deliverability resulting from low finding rates and from a lack of incentive for producers to explore for and develop new reserves because of inadequate and uncertain netback. Producers have moved drilling rigs and personnel to the United States and other areas where opportunities at this time appear to be more attractive. The decline in exploration and development activity starting two or more years ago is now being reflected in fewer reserves being available to maintain deliverability.
Further, they say:
An essential component of a solution to the problem of deliverability would appear to be a known system of pricing and a stable system of royalties and taxation adequate to provide producers with the incentive to carry out vigorous exploration and development programs.
Further, at page 86:
A further problem relates to the competition of the United States in particular, and the energy-short world in general, for drilling rigs, skilled personnel and investment funds. The uncertainty and lack of economic incentive on the Canadian scene in the past two years and the large exploration and development program under way in the

United States under more favourable incentives, have caused an exodus of equipment, men and money south of the border.
This tax has been made necessary only because the government has mismanaged the oil industry, and it is a tax that is most unpopular. It hits one segment of the motoring public that uses oil but is unfair in that it penalizes individuals who might live in areas where there is no public transport and who need their automobiles for daily commuting. It will bear more heavily on those who live in rural areas and must of necessity use their automobiles for even daily living, like trips to the grocery store.
If it has any value whatsoever, it must mean that the government should move within reason toward the world price for our highly valued oil and gas that are so very desirable. A two-price system has not prevented us from entry into a recessionary phase from which we may well be a long time emerging. Even today the industrial index has not bottomed out, and all indications are that Canada will lag far behind the United States in returning to a full-time industrial position.
During this coming recession it may well be necessary to raise the price of oil and gas to world levels, or even above, in order to encourage exploration and development of our energy sources. But, most of all, the federal government along with the provincial governments have not worked out a taxation structure that will likely ensure us a reasonably secure supply in the next few years.

Mr. Speaker, on budget night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduced a special excise tax on gasoline purchased for personal use. This ten cents a gallon tax is imposed on the producers and importers of gasoline and will be passed on to the consumer in its entirety. Provision will be made to refund the full amount of the tax on gasoline used for farming, fishing, construction, mining and most forms of commercial transportation.
There are a number of objectionable features to this tax with which I shall deal in a moment, but I suggest we cannot simply look at the tax alone. We have to look at the full range of proposals to change taxes which the minister has made and which I maintain will go a long way, by the time they are implemented, to wipe out most of the improvements in our social security system made by Liberal and Conservative governments over the last 25 years.
Let me make reference to some of the proposals of the minister. The hospital insurance plan, which was first begun by the province of Saskatchewan under a CCF government, was made a national plan really by a Conservative government which agreed to pay 50 per cent of a universal hospitalization plan that was implemented by a province. The minister has given notice that as soon as he can, the federal government will cease to pay the 50 per cent of the cost of hospitalization which it has paid since the commencement of the plan.
Similarly, in the case of medical insurance a number of provinces, particularly the province of Ontario, were, to say the least, loth to come into a medical insurance scheme. They thought that their people were adequately protected by the various voluntary plans in existence, and they felt that all they wanted from Ottawa was help in covering those people who had not seen their way clear to
July 18, 1975

joining a voluntary plan. At that time the federal government said-and I know they were right-that that was not good enough, that we must have a universal plan, one to which every citizen of a province belongs and by which he will receive protection against medical costs.
This was to be, and has been until now, a shared-cost program, with the federal government and the province each paying half. Now the minister has given notice that as soon as he can-which I think will be by 1985-Ottawa will no longer pay that 50 per cent, that there will be a limit on the amount Ottawa will pay in any year. If the increase in the actual cost is more than the federal government is prepared to pay, then obviously the provinces will have to meet the increase or cut the standard of services. The province of Manitoba calculates that its cost by the year 1985 to cover the shortfall from Ottawa for hospital and medical insurance will be between $40 million and $50 million a year. We should keep in mind that this is one of the smaller provinces.
Ottawa has been paying 50 per cent of the cost of post-secondary education, but this year that payment is being limited, in respect of an increase in any year, to a ceiling of 15 per cent. This year the provinces will receive $1181/2 million less than they would have received had the government not unilaterally imposed this ceiling. It is interesting to see that the province of Manitoba is hit the hardest. The province of Quebec, which has been faithful to the Liberal Party in electing members of parliament, this year will lose $82 million because of this unilateral decision of the federal government. The province of British Columbia will lose $20.7 million this year as a result of the decision to put a limit on the increase in respect of grants for post-secondary education.
We have heard much from Liberal prime ministers and Liberal ministers of national health and welfare about how great the Canada Assistance Plan is and the fact that it was a Liberal government which encouraged the provinces to consolidate and rationalize their social security programs under the Canada Assistance Plan. Ottawa paid 50 per cent of the cost. Now Ottawa says, quite unilaterally, that the days of the Canada Assistance Program are numbered. The federal government now proposes to replace the Canada Assistance Plan with a new series of acts including a proposed social services act. Under that act, the position of the federal government is that unless a province meets national guidelines it will not be permitted to receive 50 per cent of the cost of its programs from the federal government. That is a very worth-while objective.
If the provincial standards are lower than the standards set by the federal government, this would not be desirable, if this is one country in which we should have minimum standards which apply to every citizen regardless of where he lives. This limitation will also apply to any provinces which have programs in respect of which the standards are higher than the standards Ottawa has set for those provinces, so that the citizens of such provinces will begin to suffer as soon as Ottawa puts its intention into effect.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has been travelling from one end of the country to the other, talking very eloquently about income support
Excise Tax Act
programs and supplementation programs which the federal government proposes and in which they want the provinces to co-operate with them. Not once has the minister been willing to sit down with the provinces and estimate, with them, the cost of these programs. The programs about which he is talking may be good programs, but in light of what the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) intend to do with the shared-cost programs, it is not surprising that the provinces are at least suspicious.
Ottawa's timetable is very restrictive. The policy under the Canada Assistance Plan will go into effect in 1976-77, but the income supplementation program for the working poor, about which the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been talking, will not become effective until 1978. The time to protect people against inflation is now. The time to stimulate the economy is now. Now, when we have an unemployment figure of 8 per cent, is the time we need assistance. Yet now is the time when the federal government is beginning to put the screws on and is turning them very hard.
Let me speak for a few moments about another proposal of the minister. I refer to the proposal to increase the unemployment insurance premium. We have heard a great deal, from one end of the country to the other, both inside and outside parliament, about the supposed rip-off of the unemployment insurance plan by people who really do not want to work. I have said before, and I say again, that I am sure there are some who fall into that category. I think in cases where such people are found, they should be weeded out so that they do not receive benefits. I believe the number of people receiving benefits to which they are not entitled is not very large. I would not have been surprised had the minister come forward with proposals to try to tighten up the qualifications for benefits so that people who really are not trying to find work would not be able to obtain benefits. Although I would not have been enthused by such a proposal, I would not have been surprised.
The proposal we have from the minister, and I presume from the government as a whole, is that the premiums be increased in respect of all the people, including those who work regularly, the people with steady jobs. These people will have to pay more money every payday. These people form the backbone of this plan. Those who work regularly will have to pay for the benefits of the unemployed who to a large extent are a result of the economic policies designed by the government to create more unemployment. It could not have been a more unfair or a more regressive proposal. The minister, in effect, is taxing the wrong people through this increased unemployment insurance premium.
Let us look at the tax on gasoline. I said that it is regressive. It makes no difference whether the person concerned has an income of $6,000 a year, $30,000 a year or $60,000 a year; he or she will have to pay ten cents extra, in the form of an excise tax, on every gallon of gas used, with the exception that some people who are able to prove to the satisfaction of the Department of National Revenue that they use their cars for business will be able to obtain a refund of part of the excise tax. The percentage of the refund these people receive will depend on the type of

July 18, 1975
Excise Tax Act
deduction they make in respect of automobile expenses for purposes of calculating their income tax.
This means that a doctor can probably get a refund of this tax, so can a lawyer, an architect or a salesman. They can all get refunds on all or part of this tax. But what about the worker who has no other means of getting to work except driving his car? He has no chance at all, although he is probably in the $6,000 or $7,000 a year category, as compared to the businessman who is in the $30,000 or $50,000 a year category. But, as has always been the case with Liberal governments and Liberal finance ministers, "to those that have shall be given."
One would have thought that if we are in a situation where it is obvious that we must begin to think about a more rational use of our resources-and one of the ways of conserving our resources would be to reduce the use of gasoline-we would have had an entirely different set of proposals from the minister. We should have had a serious attempt to implement, not wild ideas advanced by wideeyed visionaries who have no practical experience with life or government, but the promises made by the Prime Minister in the election campaign last year.
Let me summarize a couple of speeches which the Prime Minister made, both of which were reported in the Montreal Gazette. On June 17, the Prime Minister, in a speech in Toronto, announced a $270 million program to aid public transit. He said the Liberal government would pay 100 per cent of the cost of Canadian-made commuter vehicles and 50 per cent of the cost of platforms and stations. The government would also pay 25 per cent of the cost of Canadian-manufactured vehicles for public transit within cities. Encouragement and assistance would be given to smaller municipalities in the creation of new transit systems. Canadian industry would be encouraged to develop passenger vehicles, and experimentation with new transit systems would be assisted by federal financing of demonstration projects.
The next day the Prime Minister was speaking in Cornwall, and he said that the Liberal government would take responsibility for rail passenger service out of the hands of CNR and CPR and entrust the task to a new Crown corporation. The corporation would run high-speed rail services in heavily populated areas such as the Windsor-Quebec City corridor, it would introduce luxurious transcontinental excursion trains and establish a super bus service between medium-sized cities.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Was that during the election?

Yes. Those were just two speeches the Prime Minister made. I wish I had more time to put on the record all the promises the Prime Minister made about what the Liberal government would do in the field of transportation. We have not seen hide nor hair of any of these promises. Has there been the slightest beginning in this respect? We do not have plans and proposals which would help the ordinary person. What we have is the kind of blunderbuss proposal that we are debating today, the ten cents tax on gasoline. One would think that ordinary citizens had a choice about whether or not they should use

their cars. I will give just one illustration from my own city of Winnipeg because I know it best.
My son-in-law lives four miles due east of where he works. He can drive to work in the morning and drive back in the afternoon in less than ten minutes. But if he wanted to co-operate with the Minister of Finance and cut down on the use of his car, and if he wanted to use the public transit system, unfortunately for him the main direction of the transit system in the city of Winnipeg is not east-west but north-south. So if he wanted to go to work using the public transit system, he would have to take a bus, transfer twice, go all the way downtown and all the way back to his place of work. It would take him-I am speaking very cautiously and conservatively-about one hour and 15 minutes at the minimum, as compared to ten minutes by car.
Did the minister give any thought to that kind of problem? Of course not. All he was concerned about was to prove to the people of Canada that he was concerned about inflation. The hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), when he spoke yesterday said, in effect, "You people in the opposition who are criticizing this tax are not facing up to the fact that this great Liberal government is pledged to protect those parts of Canada which have to to be served by imported oil, and this will help to pay the cost of subsidizing their expensive oil". What is the cost of that subsidy? It is about $350 million. The hon. member for Scarborough West said that the minister had to find the money and that is what the tax is for.
It is a laudable desire. People in the maritime provinces, the people in Quebec and all the people east of the Ottawa River should have assistance in keeping the price of oil and gas down. But was that the only place from which the minister could get the money? I do not believe that for a moment, because if one looks at the minister's budget of November, 1974, and then at his budget of June, 1975, one finds two illustrations of alternatives which the minister could have used. In his November, 1974, budget the minister extended to all corporations the fast write-off provision for the purchase of equipment. The loss of revenue to the federal government from that one measure alone, according to the minister, himself, for this current year is over $500 million. In his budget of June, 1975, the minister introduced a new investment tax credit for corporations. This will lead to a further loss of revenue to the federal government of at least $200 million this year.
In these two provisions alone the minister gave up over $700 million in revenue this year-twice as much as the minister will get from his ten cents a gallon tax. I say that that tax was, and is, unnecessary; it will bear down hardest on the people who can least afford to pay it. What will the tax mean to the ordinary citizen? It has been calculated by economists, and not challenged by the government or the minister, that the ten cents a gallon excise tax and the $1.50 increase on a barrel of crude oil, which the minister is approving, will increase the cost by 2 per cent; it will cost the motorist who drives 15,000 miles a year, and who gets 20 miles to the gallon in his car, between $75 and $90 a year to drive his car. The $1.50 a barrel increase in the price of oil will cost him $35 to $40 a year, and the cost of heating his home will increase by $60 a year. This, I assume, is just for cities such as Ottawa, Toronto, and
July 18, 1975

Montreal and does not apply to cities such as Edmonton and Winnipeg where it is much colder, and it certainly does not apply to the northern part of Canada where it is necessary to heat a home for six or more months a year.
These are the effects this excise tax will have on the ordinary citizen in this country. I have already indicated that the minister could have obtained the extra revenue he needed by not going ahead with the extra goodies he promised to corporations in the last year or two. He could also have increased the income tax. At least in theory, income tax is a progressive tax, if one can ignore all the little gimmicks which permit people in the upper income brackets to avoid paying their fair share of tax. At least in principle income tax is collected from those who are best able to pay. But no, the minister had to apply this tax which is very regressive.
The minister expressed the hope that the excise tax, combined with the increase which will be at least 5 cents per gallon and probably more, would encourage motorists to make their driving habits more efficient in terms of saving gasoline. There is no hard evidence that such price increases have anything but a temporary effect on consumption. The Statistics Canada table entitled "Canadian Crude Oil Requirements-Anticipated and Actual Refinery Receipts of Crude Oil" show that the demand for crude oil by refineries has been increasing every year and that there is a rigidity in the present patterns of gasoline consumption. From 1971 to 1975 there was an increase in refinery production from 51 million barrels to 68 million barrels-an increase of over 25 per cent. While that was happening, the price of oil was increasing from $4 to $6.50 per barrel and now it will be increased to $8 per barrel.
I could understand this if there was evidence that the oil companies needed the increases they have received over the years. Let me remind the minister that in 1971 the oil companies were receiving between $2.80 and $2.90 per barrel for western oil. They were doing very well. They were arguing that they needed price increases to expand and to explore for new oil, and so on, and they were indicating that they needed price increases of the nature of ten cents per barrel, per year, for ten years. In other words, by 1981 they would have been looking for $3.80 per barrel. Mr. Speaker, it is not 1981, it is only 1975, and they already will be receiving $8 per barrel. They are doing this because this government has refused to get involved in planning to meet our needs. We do not really know what our oil reserves are. We have to go on from year to year depending essentially on the information we obtain from the oil companies. This information has fluctuated wildly, as it suited the oil companies, for their own good and for the good of the multinational owners of these corporations, but not for the good of Canadian citizens.
A former Liberal cabinet minister, Mr. Kierans, has pointed out that the Canadian Petroleum Association published misleading statements of Canadian oil and gas reserves in 1970 in order to encourage the federal government to authorize exports to the United States. He warned that we are in a desperate situation, which we are. That desperate situation was highlighted yesterday by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) in his announcement about new restrictions on the sale and
Excise Tax Act
distribution of natural gas. Mr. Kierans warned that we are in a desperate situation because of the massive amounts of oil which we in Canada sold to the United States at $3 per barrel until last year, and we must now develop it at a probable cost of $13.70 per barrel. In 1970 the Canadian Petroleum Association estimated that Canada had 125 billion barrels of oil and 725 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, when in fact we had only 7.7 billion barrels of oil and 52.5 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
It was on the basis of that kind of information that the federal government and the National Energy Board allowed the export of up to 1.2 million barrels of oil per day and an additional 6 trillion cubic feet of natural gas to the United States in the early 1970s. Do we have any more real information now than we had in 1970 when the National Energy Board and the government permitted that disastrous sale at those ridiculous, disgracefully low prices to the United States-sales which had to be made if we were to honour contracts entered into? I am one of those who realizes that it is difficult, if not impossible, to back out of a contract made in good faith.
How did we make that decision? We made it on the recommendation of the National Energy Board. Did it have its own technical people, its own geologists, engineers and economists who were able to obtain the information and to assess it in a way which was beneficial for the people of Canada, or did it in fact depend almost exclusively on information obtained from the oil and gas companies, information which was slanted to be of benefit to those corporations and not to the people of Canada? I must ask the minister whether we are in any better position in 1975 to make the kind of decisions we ought to be making than we were in 1970. I doubt it.
When I listen to the minister-another apologist for the government-and the oil companies talk about the necessity for higher oil and gas prices, which will mean higher costs for the people of Canada, I listen in amazement and wonder on what they base their arguments. I am not an expert in business, but I can read the English language and I think I understand what I read. Since coming to Ottawa I have received the Toronto Globe and Mail every morning. I refer the Minister of Finance to an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of May 16, 1975, under the heading "Western oils turn in best profit performance in quarter with 48.1 per cent increase". What does it say in the first paragraph of that article? It reads as follows:
With a 48.1 per cent year-over-year increase, western oils turned in the best profit performance in a preliminary Report on Business survey of after-tax profits of Canadian corporations for the first quarter. They did the same thing in three of the past four quarters.
Has the minister never asked the oil companies, "Isn't enough enough"? If he has, I wish he would send me a copy of the text, because I do not remember him ever making that kind of speech. But I do remember the minister saying that workers who ask for wage increases, not of 48 per cent but of 15 and 18 per cent, to keep up with the increase in the cost of living are being unreasonable, unpatriotic and that they are going to wreck the economy.

We have had that kind of speech from the minister quite often, but we do not hear it when it comes to oil companies. They get a further increase in price. I went to the parliamentary library and got the Financial Post "Survey of Oils for 1975". I should like to put a few of the figures on the record. Hon. members know that I am one of those terrible socialists who does not have much use for the free enterprise system. Let us see what the Financial Post says about some of the oil companies. Take Imperial Oil's net income, that is, after taxes and everything else: 1971, $136 million; 1972, $151 million; 1973, $228 million; the Globe and Mail of January 24, 1975, shows their 1974 net income was $290 million.
Maybe Imperial Oil is an exception, so let us look at Gulf Canada, another poor oil company which needs that increase or it will go broke tomorrow. In 1971 they had a net income of $53 million; 1972, $64 million; 1973, $101 million. They have not released the figures for 1974, but we can be sure they are in the same "marginal" increase range as Imperial Oil.
How many employees do they have?

Of course, they have Canadian people working and Canadian customers buying their products. That is the point. Let us look at Shell Canada. In 1971 their net income was $61 million; in 1972, $78 million; 1973, $112 million. I do not have figures for 1974, but no doubt they will be in the same range as Imperial Oil.
When is enough enough, Madam Speaker? How much more do the Canadian people have to pay to keep the poor oil companies in business? The minister says that we have to give them higher oil prices, and unless we do they will not look for new oil; and if we do not find new oil, of course, we will be out of it. I think we have a right to compare the oil industry with the electric power industry.
Oh, oh!

The hon. member is always interjecting. I like to have his interjections, particularly when I am not on a 20 minute limit. But I would like to hear the hon. member make his own speech some time. I do not mind his interjections, but some members are disconcerted by his bleating.
In Manitoba they are bringing into production power from the Nelson River. That is a long way from where the power will be used. The plants and transmission lines will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and the power will probably cost three or four times as much as the power now being used in Manitoba. Ontario is building a nuclear power station whose power will cost four or five times more than the power at Niagara Falls. They do not tell the people of the province that it is going to cost four times as much for the nuclear power; therefore they want them to pay four times as much as for the cheap power they are getting now. They put the two costs together and come up with one price.
We have oil in Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the companies were making good money selling it at $3 a barrel and less. Now they want $8, $10 and $12 per barrel, not only for the new oil which they hope to find in the

Arctic or off the east coast, which will be very expensive, but they want the same price for the oil they found years ago on which they are going to make tens of millions of dollars. The minister goes along with that and says we have to give them the increased price.
The Canadian citizen is going to have to pay through the nose for every gallon of gasoline he buys for his car, for every gallon of heating oil for his home, for every cubic foot of natural gas for his home, for every bit of gas used to fuel the industries.

Madam
Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-66 which is another expose of the iniquities that this government heaps on the Canadian people.
