speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Oh, come on now. Be nice.

The weaker the argument, the more strident her voice became. She provided a lot of laughs for government members, but I can assure this House that no one is laughing in the federal riding of Skeena, at Burns Lake, Ootsa Lake, Francois Lake. They are not laughing on the streets of Smithers or Kitimat and the union shops there, or in the shopping centres at Terrace or Prince Rupert, and certainly not at Port Clements or Charlotte City. She says her riding supports the ten-cent tax. I can see it now: when she gets off the plane for the summer recess, there will be senior citizens welcoming her with bated breath to thank her for this opportunity to give the Government of Canada another ten cents per gallon for gas.
The taxi drivers will be lining up to say they have been waiting for a long time for an opportunity to pay another tax to the federal government. The fishermen and independent loggers will say, "We know that each of us cannot go to Ottawa, but in our stead you shall go to the Minister of Finance and thank him personally for this
July 18, 1975

opportunity to give another ten cents a gallon to the federal government. Tell him the people of Skeena thank the government for this opportunity."
Let us look for a moment at the impeccable flow of logic from the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) in support of this new tax. The second half of her speech criticized regional disparities in Canada. She pointed out that the west is getting short shrift and is being shoddily dealt with in confederation. She is right. For example, if you buy an airline ticket from Toronto to Ottawa, the cost is approximately $70. If you buy a ticket to fly from Vancouver to Prince George, approximately the same distance, you pay 30 per cent more, or $100. There is good example of regional disparity, and it cannot be justified.
I think all members on this side agree on the existence of regional disparity, especially between the north and south of Canada, and we say it cannot be justified. I well remember the royal commission the hon. member spoke about, the one of 1964 headed by Cyril Shelford, or inspired by Cyril Shelford when he was working for the British Columbia government. I think he got the double shuffle. I have travelled extensively in northern British Columbia and I know that the people of the region are paying too much for gasoline. I understand perfectly what the hon. member is saying, but I point out that the official opposition did not do that of which she complains. The opposition did not create that disparity. Yet the first half of the hon. member's speech was devoted almost entirely to berating the opposition. She calls our approach ostrichlike and accuses us of putting our heads in the sand. Incidentally, if she will check I think she will find that her ornithology is not quite correct.
Her speech was for the birds.

The opposition has criticized the government for that very reason. We object to this country's disparities. The question remains, why did the hon. member devote the first half of her speech to berating the opposition, when she agrees with the opposition? If she looks closely, she will find that the ostrich is coming close to her, and has come back to roost.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am delighted to note that the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) is so adept at naming places in my constituency. I wonder if he is as adept at naming places in his own. In any event, the voters of the constituency of Surrey-White Rock are asking where he stands on the issues on which he is speaking. I suggest that he should devote some time to his own people, rather than to mine, who are being looked after very well.

Madam Speaker, I remind the hon. member for Skeena that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) said in this House that the people of Surrey-White Rock are being well served by their member.
Hear, hear!
That is not exactly what he meant.

But that's what he said.
Excise Tax Act

It strikes me that there is an appropriate line in Hamlet, which could be applied to the hon. lady: "The lady doth protest too much, methinks." Near the beginning of Hamlet a character says that there is something rotten in the state of Denmark-I submit that it is not only in Denmark.
Let us consider this tax. The minister suggests that the budget is non-inflationary, that he is introducing a noninflationary tax-if there is such a thing-and non-inflationary policies. Let us examine the workings of these policies. A man came to see me and we had a long discussion about the very problem we are considering today. That man is a small businessman in my community. He runs a small bus line, and is responsible for a total payroll of $150,000. His profit margin is not wide.
I understand that rebates from the tax department are now running between six months and one year behind time. The bus company expects this tax to add $1,000 a year to costs. Because the operator is operating on a small margin of profit he will probably need to borrow that $1,000 at 14 per cent, which means that the company must pay extra expenses of $1,400. This man has to make up this cost somewhere. He cannot pull the money out of a hat, as the government seems to be able to do; therefore he must consider increased rates. He has a contract with the local school board. The school board must get its money from school taxes, and school taxes in British Columbia, as the hon. member for Skeena knows, are away beyond the reach of the individual taxpayer. The operator also runs charters for senior citizens and others.
If the bus company wants to increase its rates, it must justify the increase before the Transport Commission. The Transport Commission will not sit for three months. What is the company to do in the meantime? How is it to survive? If tax upon tax is imposed on such small companies, the only alternative they face, sooner or later, is to sell out.

Or give the company to the
government.

The owner can either sell to the government, or to a large corporation-to the sort of large, multinational corporation the hon. member berated so strongly.
Let me digress. Today the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce introduced phase II of his program which is designed to limit foreign investment. We know, I think, that most of our foreign investment comes from the United States. United States companies take over small Canadian companies which can no longer bear the kind of tax burden the government is forcing on them. Large, multinational corporations can bear the burden. They can pass on the extra cost to the consumer, but the small companies cannot hold out. And the hon. member help up Petro-Can as the panacea for all the ills brought on by the greed of large, multinational corporations. I ask this: if a bureaucrat switches from a multinational corporation to a government, does he thereby become a pillar of morality, a bastion of morality?
My socialist friends keep talking about equality, but there is one equality they always tend to overlook, the equality of human nature and man's tendency to evil. No matter whether you work for a government or a private

July 18, 1975
Excise Tax Act
corporation, temptation is there. The temptations and the greed still exists. The possibility of mismanagement is just as great, whether you work for a private corporation or for the government. Incidentally, the role of government is to exercise some control, either by passing laws or by appealing to conscience.
This new tax will entail simply another cost which large corporations can easily pass on to consumers but which small companies will not be able to cope with and, consequently, sooner or later they will sell out to large corporations.
If the tax were imposed only to conserve energy I could argue in support of it, on condition that the motorist is provided with an alternative.
One year ago I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promising a $1 billion urban transport policy. The Prime Minister promised that, when travelling across the country. We were wafted to the Elysian fields by the Prime Minister's dulcet tones promising answers to our transportation headaches.
Do you like poetry?
I love poetry. Does the hon. member prefer John Donne, Shakespeare, Spencer, Chaucer or Matthew Arnold? Take your pick.
We will take the hon. member, the bard of White Rock. He is just great.

Yes, the Prime Minister made a memorable trip across the country one year ago. Incidentally, about the only time he crosses this country is during election campaigns. The rest of the time he likes to go to places like Bermuda, Switzerland, and so on. Since that trip we have heard no word about alternatives for the motorist. He must now pay this tax, this unfair tax, and he has no alternative. The commuter who moved from the heart of the city to get away from the problems of urbanization, or because he wanted cheaper housing, is now forced to pay an extra $1, $1.50 or $2 per week in tax, just because he tried to save a buck. There is no way we can justify this.
Let me make one more point-I am sure this will come as a relief to government members. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) promised a reduction in the rate of bureaucratic growth. That is the absolute conundrum in the face of-
That's a nice word.
Nice, isn't it?
Yes, it is very nice.

I will use it again. That is an absolute conundrum in the face of the refund policy the Minister of Finance wants to impose on the country. He says he wants to reduce the growth of the bureaucracy from 9,300 to 6,000. Much against my nature, I would simply caution that the minister will need that army of bureaucrats to shuffle the papers and get out the rebates within a year. They will be needed for income tax.
[Mr. Friesen.)

I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-66. The regressive measures embodied in this bill, for example the excise tax on gasoline, the air transportation tax, and the other inadequacies of the

easure such as the removal of the sales tax on insulation *fleet the failure of the budget which the minister *ought down last June.
The over all impact of the budget on the Canadian :onomy has been adequately described by previous leakers. The inflationary effect of the budget, including le excise tax on gasoline, the degree of unemployment lat will result from the budgetary items, and the negative feet it will have on the growth of the gross national roduct, are all part of the record. However, the notable *ature about the budget has not been the technical anal-sis of the effect it will have on inflation, unemployment, r the gross national product, but the instantaneous nega-ve reaction of the working man and woman, those on low nd fixed incomes.
I do not recall when my correspondence and telephone ills have been heavier or busier with constituents regis-?ring legitimate complaints about the discriminatory spects of the budget and the dire consequences it will ave on their future.
I am certain the minister must be receiving similar omplaints from his constituents, and indeed from across 'anada. I have no intention of reading the correspondence ito Hansard, but it may be useful to the minister in his eassessment of the budget if I mention the nature of the omplaints received.
Not unexpectedly the major objection is related to the pecial excise tax of ten cents per gallon on gasoline for ersonal use, with an exemption for industrial and commercial users through rebates. I will have more to say bout that later.
The second matter that has been brought to my atten-ion is the increase in unemployment insurance premiums ffective early in 1976, plus other proposed measures, in >articular those related to employees retiring, which pro-losals are meeting with opposition.
Although the removal of the sales tax on insulation naterial has received minimal notice, the reaction to the nadequacies of budgetary matters related to housing are lotable.
The increase in the wellhead price of oil and the ncreased price of natural gas, with their obvious impact >n the average consumer struggling against the relentless ncrease in inflation, are of concern to my constituents ind, what is more important, they are faced with the ealization and fear that the government cannot or will mot introduce measures to reverse this feeling of lelplessness.
I want to turn to a very important matter in the budget, *nergy. The adverse effects that the energy proposals, ncluding the excise tax of 10 cents, will have on inflation ind unemployment, have been stressed by previous speak-;rs. It has been estimated that the measures introduced by he minister will add two points to the consumer price ndex and, in Ontario alone, will cost the citizens an idditional $700 million annually.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in presenting his judget indicated that the price of crude oil must rise to [DOT]vorld price levels. He also emphasized the policy of a iingle national price for crude oil. I can accept the argu-nents in principle. He made reference to the importance
Excise Tax Act
of a conservation program. I agree with and accept in principle the policy of a single national price for crude oil. I will mention later than I think the minister has taken a most discriminatory route to accomplish this. I have no difficulty in recognizing that there should be differences in terms of variations in price with respect to transportation costs.
I would support a program that encourages exploration and development to ensure continuing supplies to all Canadians. I would welcome and encourage a more aggressive program in research and development. I would respond in a positive fashion if the government truly demonstrated leadership in the development of a conservation program. I can understand the arguments to maintain a world price for export.
However, having made these observations, one might reasonably have expected that the budget would have contained measures designed to assure Canadians of energy supplies, measures to ensure further exploration or to promote something tangible by way of research and development; or we might have looked for a bolder and more imaginative conservation policy. But it is impossible to find any such proposals in the budgetary measures.
Further, what the minister has failed to explain, and what such a policy of world price fails to recognize, is that foreign oil-producing countries have established artificially higher prices, producing massive cash surpluses. Many thoughtful Canadians reject the necessity of Canadian consumers being exploited in the purchase of their own resources so as to maintain an artificial world price. The minister has a responsibility to explain in more detail the simplistic approach of adopting an artificial world price figure, particularly at a time of rapid increase in inflation and growing unemployment.
Earlier in the debate the Minister of Finance was very critical of the province of Ontario, in particular of its attitude toward energy matters. In my view the Ontario minister of finance acted responsibly by coming to the defence of the working man and woman, and of those living on fixed incomes.
Hear, hear!

I wish to commend the comments made by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) of the New Democratic Party in his defence of Ontario and its responsible attitude toward energy matters over the years. It should not be forgotten that Ontario has supported a national oil policy for 11 years simply to stimulate the development of the oil and gas industry in Canada. I find it deplorable that the government should ignore this when it finds it convenient to do so.
As I indicated earlier, a major part of my correspondence and of the phone calls I am receiving concerns the excise tax of ten cents a gallon on gasoline for personal use. There is no question that this is a most discriminatory tax measure. Indeed, it is the most discriminatory and oppressive tax I have seen since coming to Ottawa in 1972. The minister tells us that such action is required to close the gap between the payments needed to hold down the

July 18, 1975
Excise Tax Act
cost of imported oil for eastern consumers and the revenues from the charge on oil exports to the United States.
I have no difficulty in accepting the principle of a one-price policy for Canada, but surely it is obvious to the minister that under his proposals the burden of carrying out this policy will be shouldered by those who can least afford it. As I indicated previously, I have received substantial representation strongly protesting this regressive measure. As one might expect, protestations came from men and women living in small towns and villages who drive, in many instances, more than 50 miles to and from work. They are excellent citizens, they work regularly, and they wish nothing more than to be able to raise their families in a small town or rural setting. What is the minister's answer to this? What is the penalty he exacts? It is a gasoline tax of ten cents a gallon. Surely the minister is aware of the difficulty many small towns are experiencing in maintaining their viability. This is simply another measure which will tend to add to the exodus of some inhabitants from the rural areas.
It has been suggested that car pools could be used to counteract any hardship. But this method of transportation was in use long before the introduction of the ten cents tax. Many people are already using it to counteract the spiralling increase in the cost of living. It must be obvious, too, that pleas for a rapid transit system would have little relevance to people living in an area such as my own.
I cannot accept a one-price crude oil policy the cost of which must be borne by the working man or woman and other individuals who live on fixed or low incomes. Of all the options available to the minister as a means of maintaining a one-price policy, he has chosen the most discriminatory and regressive.
The minister also gave us to understand that this tax measure was intended to encourage immediate conservation of gasoline. Surely the minister cannot be serious in believing that the introduction of an excise tax amounting to ten cents a gallon will conserve energy. He should realize that previous increases in gasoline prices have not reduced consumption. Indeed, statistics confirm that there was an increase in consumption at the same time as prices were rising.
The simple fact is that the automobile remains and will continue to be the most essential and important mode of transportation in the foreseeable future despite glowing reports about the possibilities of rapid transit systems and other modes of travel. I have no doubt Canadians will respond to a reasonable and responsible program designed to conserve energy but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that they will not accept this as a true conservation measure; they will recognize the proposal for what it is-a guise for collecting tax dollars for the federal coffers.
I wish to make a few brief remarks with respect to the imposition of the tax at producer and importer levels. The minister, in introducing his discussion paper on commodity taxation, was obviously aware of existing pricing systems and the inequities introduced by imposing taxes at the manufacturers' level. It must be apparent to the minister that his decision to place the excise tax on producers and importers means that the ten cents a gallon increase is likely to be 11 cents or 12 cents in future months.

During the course of this debate several members have drawn attention to the administrative nightmare which would be involved in supervising and policing the refund program. The minister, with some justification, has declined to comment on the size of the bureaucracy that will be needed, or on the cost which will be incurred in the handling of such a program. I use the words "with some justification" because I have contacted the Department of National Revenue seeking answers to questions asked by constituents regarding eligibility for exemption. And the department does not know the answers.
I find it ironical that earlier this week the government House leader should have been pleading with the opposition parties to deal quickly with this bill, implying that any hold-up in its passage would result in a delay in the payment of refunds, responsibility for which would then fall on opposition members. I wish to congratulate my hon. friend from Peace River for pointing out that under the Financial Administration Act, section 17 as I recall, it is possible for the government to proceed with these rebates.
If the government House leader is truly interested in relieving the taxpayer and reducing the numbers of an unproductive bureaucracy he would encourage the Minister of Finance to withdraw this iniquitous bill rather than call for its speedy passage. As I say, I can appreciate the minister's reluctance to discuss the administrative cost of this program, particularly following the announcement that the growth of the public service was to be reduced. He knows perfectly well that the administration of this program will be a severe blow to any program of restraint. Indeed, I read an article during the past week or two that appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail, indicating that the administration of the program will require at a minimum 1,000 people, and a multimillion dollar price tag.
The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock referred in his speech to the difficulty with the rebate. I have had a similar experience this past week and I think it is analogous to what we will be experiencing with this measure in the future. I refer specifically to the beef industry assistance program. May I remind hon. members that this program covered the period from March 16, 1974, to April 30, 1975, and it was a support program with a price of $23.21 a hundredweight for grades D-l, D-2, D-3 and D-4 cows.
This past weekend I had a call from a constituent who sold cows in November of last year, and again in January of this year, but has received no word about the subsidy payment. On returning I checked with the department this week, and not one payment has been made since the introduction of this program. More than that, the staff had increased by 400 per cent during this period. It is not difficult to realize the magnitude of the proposed program that the Minister of Finance has talked about and the difficulties that we can experience, when a program of the magnitude of the beef industry assistance program has obviously been an absolute failure.
Another measure that I referred to earlier was the removal of the sales tax on insulation. Although a modest step in the right direction, once again it is a symptom of the inadequacy of the June budget. If there was one area that justified the intervention of the federal government
July 18, 1975

in a meaningful way for both economic and social reasons, it was certainly in the area of housing.
In response to this critical problem the minister has simply injected funds which do not meet half of Ontario's needs to correct the housing crisis that exists in Canada. Yet these funds are expected to resolve the entire problem. In addition, in this particular bill we have the introduction of the removal of the sales tax on insulation. Surely, as indicated in the past, it would be more prudent for the government to have eliminated the remaining 5 per cent sales tax on all building materials.
When the minister reduced the 11 per cent sales tax it was indicated during argument at that time that the entire tax should be removed because the cost involved in administering the program would not be commensurate with the net gain. We also pointed out that the removal of the entire tax would have a very positive effect upon the housing situation in Canada.
What is happening at the moment, Madam Speaker? With the introduction of this new tax measure, obviously the revenue accruing to the government will be somewhat less. Yet we know that the same administrative cost will be present. However, we must recognize that there will be additional administrative costs to the housing supply industry to handle this tax exemption, and it will therefore negate to a great extent some of the effect of the 5 per cent sales tax reduction. As I said a moment ago, it would surely have made far more sense to eliminate the 5 per cent sales tax on all building materials.
I expressed earlier the disappointment that has been experienced, certainly in my area, and the concern that has been expressed over the budgetary aspects in relation to housing. Despite the removal of the tax on insulation and other budgetary matters, there will be little effect on the supply side of mortgage funding, and almost negligible effect on the stimulation of housing starts.
The inadequacy of the proposals is quite obvious and has been outlined by many members, both during the budget debate and in this debate. As I indicated earlier, the $200 million allocation does not even constitute 50 per cent of Ontario's repeated requests and demands for additional funding commitments. For the first five months of 1975 housing starts were projected to be 176,000. The additional $200 million increase will provide for approximately 7,500 new starts. I would point out to the minister, as I am sure he is aware, that this combined figure falls short by 13.6 per cent of the government's goal of 210,000 starts, and 25.9 per cent short of the Economic Council's suggestion.
Both the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of Finance have cited soaring land costs and the unavailability of serviced land as two of the major causes accounting for the poor housing situation. Yet as I interpret the budget, no provision is made for municipal funding which will be necessary in order to release serviced land on to the market or to abate the escalating cost of land.
Another feature in the budget that concerns me is the $1,200 mortgage subsidy to builders for home construction, and the $900 subsidy for rental accommodation. As I understand this subsidy program, it terminates on March 31, 1976. In effect, the government is attempting to lure
Excise Tax Act
potential home owners into the housing market with attractive mortgage subsidies, but again, as I understand it, there is no provision for continuing financial support.
I think a very valid question must be asked here. What happens come March 31 when the home owner is suddenly faced with a $50 a month increase in his mortgage payment? I ask, will the Minister of Finance be there to assist him with this particular measure?
I am glad to see that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is in the Chamber because he and the government have attempted to justify the reduced activity in the housing market on the basis of the success of the AHOP program. However, because of the income and dwelling cost restrictions of this program, a large number of people qualifying for AHOP are unable to purchase a single family dwelling. There is also growing evidence that private AHOP is not being well received and is not expected to result in a significant net addition to the funding supply as it will be largely funded from money already earmarked for housing.
In summary, Madam Speaker, I have tried to point out those matters of particular concern to the constituency I represent. In particular I have emphasized that the excise tax on gasoline is a most discriminatory and regressive tax measure. I have also tried to point out the inadequacies of the budget in the field of housing, and a symptom of this inadequacy of the budget is the reduction of the sales tax on insulation. As I have indicated, I very strongly suggest that the Minister of Finance reconsider this particular bill and remove this iniquitous taxation that is before us at the present time.

Madam Speaker, I want to take brief part in this debate because I think that what is being perpetrated upon the House of Commons, and more particularly upon the people of Canada, is not simply a measure that is very nearly fraudulent when it is said it is the only way revenues can be raised, but is also a measure that is very unfair. It is as inequitable in its application as any measure that could be devised by a government to hit the little guy. This tax hits the little guy who is not in a position to pass on his costs, and provides havens for people who might be able to hide their cost under this clause and claim benefits for professional or other reasons.
It is a grotesquely unfair bill. I am not surprised that only a scattered few backbench members on the government side have had the courage to defend this bill because they know their constituents read the record, and when their constituents read that they have defended the ten cents Turner tax which applies unfairly to the poor and those who cannot shift it off, they know that their chances of being re-elected to this House diminish. If they dispute this statement, let them get up and defend this iniquituous tax which applies unfairly to those least able to bear it.
Today I wish to speak about two aspects of this measure. The first is the conservation aspect, so-called. The second is the unfairness of the impact. I want to speak in constituency terms because all of us come from constituencies. Many of us would prefer to be back at our constituencies,

July 18, 1975
Excise Tax Act
and if the government would come to its senses and devise a fair way to meet its revenue problems we would be able to get back more quickly.
I do not want to start speaking immediately about the impact of this tax on my constituency. I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) left the House a few moments ago. I passed him on the stairway and invited him back to hear my remarks, but he declined the opportunity. I want to draw attention to the very real problems this ten cents Turner tax causes the constituents of Ottawa-Carleton, to take one example, because the constituency which is represented by the Minister of Finance is one which, among other things, contains commuters who must drive from where they live to their work, whether it be from Cumberland, Vars, Russell, Navan, Sarsfield or Orleans, whether their work be in this city or elsewhere. As I understand it they will not be able to claim this as an expense. The burden of the extra ten cents will fall straight on the shoulders of the people who must commute to work from the communities in the constituency of the minister.
What is particularly inequitable about this is that if these individuals want to come to Ottawa to see their Member of Parliament they would have to pay ten cents a gallon extra for that privilege of seeing him, but if the minister deigns to go to see his constituents-and perhaps he does not do that very often now that he has brought in this unfair tax which lies particularly heavily upon the commuters and people in the villages I have enumerated- he will probably travel in a Government of Canada limousine and will not have to bear the burden of the tax. This is not a tax for the minister but is a tax for his constituents. That is a most unfair situation.
Before leaving the subject of the constituency of Ottawa-Carleton I might say that if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) were to visit Navan, to take one place as an example, not only would there be a cost involved to the people who might drive to Navan to see this magnetic personality but also to the Government of Canada, particularly the Department of National Defence, which probably would have to pay for the helicopter that is the preferred way of travel of this conservation minded Prime Minister.
Let me deal for a moment with some of the very severe problems this unfair tax imposes upon the people in the constituency I represent. There are constituents of mine who commute distances of 150 miles per day in order to get to and from their work. They will not be in a position to claim any rebate or to shift the burden of this ten cents tax. The example I have given is perhaps an extreme one. It represents the distance from Whitecourt to Swan Hills and back. However, there are constituents of mine, and there are constituents of many other members, whether they be in urban or rural areas, who will have to pay through the nose in order to meet this unfair tax that lies particularly upon the little guy, the one who cannot cast off the tax under some kind of write-off.
Indeed in my constituency some of the individuals who are commuting are forced to commute because of a federal policy. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which is responsible for our national parks, has laid down a directive that Banff and Jasper may not

grow too large, and therefore many people must live elsewhere such as in Hinton or Canmore, and drive from there to work and then back home again at night. That situation was difficult enough at the best of times, but is now much more difficult because of this unfair ten cents tax which will be imposed upon these people very soon. It is a grotesquely unfair tax.
I received a letter the other day from a lady in Montreal who is very much concerned about conservation matters. She devotes a great deal of her time to voluntary work in an attempt to stop the government following some of the policies that offend the environment of Canada. In doing this work she is not in a position to claim any relief in the sense that it is charitable work. She does this work voluntarily, as a concerned Canadian. She made a calculation that, since she is a woman who has very little income and does not have any prospect of ever holding down a big job unless the Prime Minister should appoint her to a royal commission, or something like that, she will have to cut her voluntary work in half because she cannot afford to carry on under the extra burden of this tax.
One might say that is an isolated case, but all of us know that most of the valuable work done in the name of public service in this country is done by individual volunteers who do not work for a large organization, and are not in a situation in which they can claim a tax advantage. These people work out of the goodness of their hearts and now, because of this tax, they will be faced with an additional burden. This tax amounts to a tax on volunteer-ism in Canadian society. It will undercut the capacity of individual Canadians who want to help improve their local community or neighbourhood, or help bring forward important points in respect of public issues. These people are seriously undercut in respect of the capability to do this. This is a very serious aspect of this bill.
I notice that when the minister spoke the other night he said that the tax did not apply to hospital or similar boards. What does the minister intend to do in respect of the members of local hospital boards and other such boards in rural districts in my constituency, and in the constituencies of many vocal members on this side of the House, and in the constituencies of many of the silent members on the other side of the House? They have to travel literally hundreds of miles a week to carry out their civic responsibilities. Unless there is some way-and it would require some gymnastics in bookkeeping and accounting which would probably be beyond even the manipulators of this government-for the government to recompense those individuals, inevitably there will be demands for increases in expense allowances by members of these local boards.
Again you can say that this is a trivial thing, but it is not so trivial when it happens in country after county and municipality after municipality across this country, and when the cost is taken from the already too scarce funds of hospital boards, municipal authorities, and groups of this kind. That is another harmful blow that this ten cents Turner tax will strike at the people of my constituency and I am sure at the people in the constituencies of other members of the House, including the silent, aquiescent members on the government side.
July 18, 1975
We are not silent.

I am pleased to see that my colleague, the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) is entering the debate. I hope he will rise later today, or when the debate carries on next week or next month, and have the courage to defend this bill, because so far there have been very few backbenchers, and no ministers apart from the guy carrying the can, the poor Minister of Finance, to defend this bill.
Tell us the good side of the story.

(Rocky Mountain) My friend knows that I would tell him the good side of the story if there were one, but I cannot because there is not.
There have been a number of individuals who have already spoken in the House about the bureaucratic problems which will be encountered in trying to work out any system of rebates for those who might deserve them.
Not being a member of the government I have no cause to be afraid of my constituents, so the other day I went from door to door in my constituency and asked people what was troubling them and what I could do to help. I found that 50 per cent of the people I encountered in one town stopped me and asked how they could get around this ten cents tax, and in what way they could become eligible for some rebate. I warn the government that however clever and ingenuous it thinks it might be in working out systems of rebate, it has awakened a remarkable wave of ingenuity in the country, and that people will try to find out some way of escaping the burden of this unfair tax and put themselves in the position of the Minister of Finance, who is not going to pay it, and of doctors and other professionals who will find some way of evading it.
What is bad about that is not that people's ingenuity has been inspired, because this country owes much more to the ingenuity of its private citizens than it does to the policies of the government, but that people are being required to turn their ingenuity not to a respect for the law but to a way of getting around it. That is another very dangerous social consequence that falls from a bill as bad as this bill.
There is not much time left this afternoon, and I want to deal for a moment with the argument which has not been put forward very strongly, even by ministers of the Crown who are accustomed to putting forward weak arguments with great force, and that is the argument that this is in some way or other a conservation measure.
That argument debases the cause of conservation.
The Government of Canada, and all of us in the House know that the days of cheap energy are gone, the days when we can waste our resources. But if the government were serious about devising a policy of conservation, it would have started with something else than a ten cents tax that applies unfairly to the weakest elements of society. If it were serious about turning people away from the excessive use of automobiles, it would have given high priority to the development of alternative methods of transportation, but it has not done that. If it were serious, it would have devised other means to relieve high consumption. If it were serious, it would have established a general policy of conservation. The conservation policy of
Business of the House
the government is one part a comic book which tells Canadians not to bathe, and one part a bunch of public relations ads which carry the smiling image of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald).
That frightens me.

As my colleague says, this simply serves to frighten people. It probably frightens them so much that they get out from the library where they were reading that ad and go and take a drive around, thus wasting more gas.
That is the extent of the conservation policy of the government. For the minister to argue that he is advancing the ethic of conservation by bringing in a ten cents tax which applies unfairly across the country to people who cannot afford to pay it, and who cannot find any way to evade it, a tax which, in addition, has the unfortunate consequence of causing problems in rural areas and local municipalities for people who have to commute, is simply a fraudulent approach.

One of the measures in which many of us across the country are interested, including many provincial governments, is the decentralization of industry and other activities to communities outside major centres. If we are going to impose this tax on people who have no other way to get from where they live to where they work, on people who commute, it will seriously frustrate the policy of decentralization to which many of the governments, including some governments of the stripe of the government here, if they still admit to kinship, are committed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Elmer M. MacKay (Central Nova) moved
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CONFER CONSTITUTIONAL REFERENCE RIGHTS ON CITIZENS
speechtext:
that Bill C-239, to amend the Supreme Court Act (private citizen's reference), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Madam Speaker, this bill is intended to emphasize that each and every citizen has a unique and personal interest in the constitution of our great nation and an individual interest in the way in which he or she is governed since, by long tradition, each Canadian has the right to expect consideration of individual rights and freedoms. Therefore each citizen ought to have a means to act directly to protect his or her interest without necessarily waiting for a government, federal or provincial, to do it.
It seems that at this particular time our government is not sufficiently conscientious in referring matters, in which constitutionality could be an issue, to our Supreme Court regardless of the implications of its failure to do so. As one example, I cite the situation arising out of a
|Mr. Lefebvre.]
current piece of legislation, Bill C-2, known by those who are most familiar with it as the competition act.
As far back as 1973 the government was well aware that there were possible constitutional difficulties and in one of its publications, "Proposals for a New Competition Policy for Canada," the following appears:
While the constitutionality of new section 31.1 may be challenged as relating to property and civil rights or matters of a local or private nature which, under section 92 of the B.N.A. Act, are within provincial, rather than federal, jurisdiction, it is nevertheless hoped that the section will be upheld as a matter ancillary to the criminal law-
In debates of the other place, as reported in Hansard for Wednesday, March 19, 1975, Senator Hayden, when speaking about certain aspects of Bill C-2, said that the Senate Committe on Banking, Trade and Commerce was concerned about the doubtful constitutionality relating, and I quote:
-to the proceedings under Part IV. 1. This was also mentioned in submissions, inlcuding that of the Canadian Bar Association-
I do not intend to smuggle a speech on Bill C-2, into this private member's hour, in case that was the suspicion but I am merely using it as an example of a case where a constitutional matter has some bearing, in my opinion, on this bill, which is in my name.
Still later in April of this year, during proceedings of the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, an official of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Mr. Bertrand, spoke about certain aspects of the constitutionality of Bill C-2. At the same time a legal consultant to the committee, Mr. R. J. Cowling, acknowledged that representations were made to the committee suggesting that the constitutional question, and I quote:
-should be settled before the bill is enacted so that a private litigant would not be left with the burden of testing the provisions all the way to the Supreme Court, which could be quite costly and perhaps even ruinous for that individual.
Finally, the chairman of the committee, the Hon. Salter A. Hayden, made a very significant observation when he said the following:
We simply point out the areas in which there is doubtful constitutional validity-so doubtful that we think they should not come into law until that doubt has been resolved.
It seems that our Supreme Court ought to be used more and ought to be more easily accessible and at less cost to the ordinary citizens of this country, and I have some support for my contention from lawyers across the country. If I may, I would like to read briefly an excerpt from a letter I received from a prominent Ontario lawyer, who wrote the following:
Dear Mr. MacKay:
I would like to lend my support to your proposal that the Supreme Court Act be amended to allow private citizens to refer questions to the Court relating to any public law made by or under the authority of the Parliament of Canada.
Judges in this country, and no doubt in others too, have many times declared themselves opposed to any development in the law that they consider would have the effect of increasing the workload on the Court. A recent instance of course is the refusal to hear Mr. Thorson's application for a ruling on a constitutionality of the legislation on bilingualism.
I think it is time the Courts were informed that their services are required in this area.
July 18, 1975

I do not necessarily share the opinion of the solicitor who wrote to me in respect to the special example he used, but I do think it is significant that a practising lawyer would voluntarily support the concept embodied in this bill.
I anticipate that some of my colleagues this afternoon will say that this legislation will increase the workload of the Supreme Court and that there will be cases where matters would be referred to the court which, in the name of common sense, ought not to be. In response to such observations it may be said that in a democratic country such as ours there are bound to be cases where people will act to protect themselves without considering all the implications of what they are doing, but I suggest most strongly that this is not a weakness. It is a strength that a democracy is, by its nature, less rigid and more indulgent in granting its citizens a means to express publicly their dissent in the advancement of their rights, and this is what I am seeking to promote by this legislation.
The court can, by the application of its own rules, or, if necessary, by changing the rules with approval of government, sort out and dispense with those cases which are frivolous or vexatious in their objects, and still permit access to the Supreme Court of our country to those who have an important issue for adjudication.
I do not wish to speak at great length on this bill, preferring rather to put it before my colleagues for informed comment and consideration. In my opinion this bill does not impinge on any provincial rights, and it might act as a catalyst to cause some provincial administrations to consider some of their own rules of civil procedure.
This bill does provide for notice of hearings to be given to the proper federal and provincial officials in appropriate instances, and provides as well that the court has the power to give notice to interested persons and classes who might be affected. There is also provision for the situation where there may be unascertained classes-the unborn, for example-and the court may, in its discretion, request any counsel to represent such parties.
As the public service becomes larger, and as the doctrine which some call collectivism grows more popular, at the expense of the traditional respect for the individual and his rights, it becomes more important to have the services of our Supreme Court available in appropriate cases so that our court can come easily to the aid of Canadians who are the victims of expediency, or of big, impatient governments.
There is much to be said for the proposition that, as the power of the state grows at the expense of the private sector, the principal menace of the common man is not the large, greedy corporation or the dictatorial or corrupt union executives or leaders, but his own over officious, bureaucratically oriented government.
Therefore I hope that if this proposal contained in my bill does not find favour with my colleagues at this time, it may be the basis for a similar move by government in the not too distant future, because I feel that a step such as this would reinforce and supplement the aims and objectives of the Canadian Bill of Rights.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CONFER CONSTITUTIONAL REFERENCE RIGHTS ON CITIZENS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I took great pleasure in studying Bill C-239 today: I had the distinct impression of being back at the university, attending a seminar on constitutional law. I feel that, for a Friday afternoon, we are dealing with a most interesting and edifying subject.
Before I start, I should perhaps bring up some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) when he was referring to Bill C-2 which he claims is anticonstitutional. He suggested that bill should be referred to the Supreme Court for a decision. To my mind, he is wrong because, as we see it, Bill C-2 is very much constitutional, both from the point of view of the powers given to the government and that of the power of law and order stipulated in the bill in question. But that is a mere digression.
Bill C-239 would grant the citizens the right to refer constitutional matters, in other words the right of referral, pertaining to federal laws, to the Supreme Court with a view to obtaining its opinion on such matters. Now, as we know, under Supreme Court Act section 55, at the present time the Attorney General of Canada, that is to say the federal government alone has the right to refer a constitutional matter to the Supreme Court for a decision.
In order to better understand the reasons which prevailed in having section 55 inserted in the Supreme Court Act, it might be well to summarize this history of the Supreme court itself, and the British North America Act which gives the Supreme Court its powers and mandate.
In 1875 the Supreme Court by an act of the Parliament of Canada under Section 101 of the British North America Act was to have a general power of appeal. It was not to be a constitutional court as such but was to be given a general power of appeal on all matters of either civil, common, or penal law, or if constitutional issues arose out of a specific case introduced before a court of common law, civil or penal jurisdiction. But in principle a purely constitutional matter could not be referred because that was not provided for in the British North America Acts.
Indeed, the federal government at that time would have liked very much for this constitutional power to be put in the constitutive instruments of the Supreme Court. Unfortunately, that was not possible for several reasons, mainly the antagonism, indifference, and even refusal of certain provinces to grant the Supreme Court that right to examine constitutional issues, and more particularly the validity of certain federal or provincial legislation.
Furthermore, it must be remembered that at that time there was another very important judicial body, even more important than the Supreme Court-the Privy Council-which had the power in last resort to decide on matters submitted to the courts. In other words, that was the highest court in Canada at that time. It suited everyone at that time, particularly Lower Canada-Quebec-to let the Privy Council have the power of adjudication in the constitutional area because if that right of adjudication on constitutional matters had been left to the Supreme Court injustices could then have taken place in the opinion of Quebeckers or Quebec political representatives, in the application of constitutional laws and the jurisdiction of

July 18, 1975
Supreme Court Act
the provinces in their relationships with the federal government.
To counter somewhat that lack of power of the Supreme Court in the constitutional area, the federal government of that time nearly imposed an additional jurisdiction upon the Supreme Court. It had to accept an ad hoc reference power in practice under which the Attorney General of Canada could refer to the Supreme Court and its judges for decisions on matters involving the constitution, matters concerning the validity of provincial legislation, matters involving federal-provincial relations, and even issues concerning interprovincial relations.
I repeat, that this power was nearly forced on the Supreme Court because, in principle, this power exceeds the powers allowed in the British North America Act, and it is very important to understand this when studying Bill C-239, which simply extends the powers conferred on the Supreme Court by section 55 of the act, which is the power of reference. Indeed, everyone knows that as concerns strictly provincial acts, provincial attorneys cannot refer constitutional matters to the Supreme Court; they must refer them to their own Supreme Court, that is, the Appeals Court in Quebec and the Provincial Supreme Court in Ontario.
Hon. members know that in 1949, the powers of the Privy Council as the court of last resort in Canada were abolished and, in practice, the Supreme Court was given supreme power in constitutional matters. Once again, I emphasize the use of the expression "in practice" because, legally, it is not a constitutional court, but a general court. I say "in practice" because there was no other instrument or agency empowered to resolve constitutional problems; the Supreme Court received these powers in 1949. This new power conferred to the Supreme Court caused concern, and maybe justifiably so, to the provinces which, in their relations with the government and the various jurisdiction conflicts which have occurred throughout the decades, had to refer such problems to a court created by the central power, whose judges were appointed by that central power and which could not finally shift in its interpretation of the legislation and more especially of jurisdictions between the federal and provincial governments. The doubts and problems of the provinces as to the real fair-mindness of the Supreme Court in fact has given rise to various federal-provincial conferences.
At first, the Quebec government took the lead. In 1950, at a federal-provincial conference, the Quebec delegation clearly stated that the Supreme Court should only be an arbitration body and as such, the provinces should be entitled to show more interest than they do at the present time, even in 1975, in the appointment or in the process for the appointment of the judges or members of that superior constitutional organization.
The Quebec delegation then stated:
We consider that the Supreme Court of Canada in constitutional matters and in Canadian intergovernmental relations must fulfil all the requirements of an arbitrator.


Quebec had realized by then, maybe a little too late, the dangers of leaving that agency of the central power, the federal government, with the last say or the last decision with respect to jurisdictional disputes between provinces and the central government, in other words, with respect to the interpretation of the British North America Acts. The province of Quebec went on with its action, and the Tremblay Commission which had been appointed by the government of Quebec at the time came up with an argumentation with the thrust on two mainstays or central elements. Those two mainstays were actually the fact that the court in question-the Supreme Court-emanated from the central power, and since there was no provision in the Constitution, in the British North America Acts, with respect to that power of adjudication in constitutional matters, Parliament must necessarily increase ad hoc, in the facts, by and by, step by step, the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in constitutional matters. This was a very progressive process, and a process which, once again, is provided for nowhere in the British North America Act.
The constitutional powers of the Supreme Court only stem from a series of over 180 decisions on constitutional matters which by and by created precedents and established the powers of the Supreme Court with respect to constitutional problems. It should actually be remembered that the decisions of the Supreme Court and the resulting recommendations when it is submitted a legal matter or a point of law for adjudication, do not have any legal binding power. They are only a means of trying to convince governments. Provinces are not bound in any way to accept the recommendations of the Supreme Court. There is, therefore, an important gap to be filled in that respect.
The second element of the findings of the Tremblay Commission was to the effet that, since Supreme Court judges are appointed by the central government, their decisions had to be, consciously or unconsciously, unfair to provinces. That is a trivial matter, but anyway a new process had to be found for appointments, possibly from a pool or through consultations with the provinces, I don't know. The Commission then said:
It would be sufficient, for example, to establish the custom of appointing to it former deputies or federal ministers. It would have been satisfactory if it had only been a matter of judging ordinary civil and criminal cases, but in constitutional conflicts it is neither normal nor satisfactory that a single party choose, appoint, and pay all the arbitrators.

Then followed a whole series of recommendations which remained ineffective for a number of years, because of a misunderstanding between federal promises, misunderstanding which is notorious over the years, since it repeated itself during the 1960 conference, when the then premier, Jean Lesage, presented once again the same arguments, and during the famous conference of Victoria when, once again, attempt was made to restore the situation in order to enable the provinces to have a consultation right in the process of nominating members of the Supreme Court.
July 18, 1975

So, the bill before us today, Bill C-239, is designed to increase the powers of reference by putting them in the Supreme Court Act, to give individuals the opportunity to refer directly to the Supreme Court matters affecting them and regarding the constitution or the validity of legislation.
I feel that under the constitutive powers and statutes of the Supreme Court as they now exist, nothing may be done because that constitutional power does not actually exist in right but is simply an extension of a general appeal procedure as confirmed under BNA Act section 101. I feel that if we broaden such competency by adding provisions to section 55, provisions that would prove theoretically valid, we would be granting the Supreme Court a jurisdiction to which it is not entitled. In fact, such action would be unjustifiable, and I am not speaking here of the additional work that this would entail for Supreme Court judges, but rather strictly from the standpoint of the interpretation of our constitution which should not permit, in my opinion, that the Supreme Court be granted these new powers, as suggested to us today by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). This being said, we do not mean to wave aside the arguments of our colleague from the opposition party.
We have no constitutional court in Canada, which is a deficiency. Could we possibly institute a Supreme Court with constitutional jurisdiction, as in the United States? We all know that the U.S. supreme court has only a power of reference strictly in the constitutional law area. It is not empowered to receive evidence. If, for instance, a case is brought before a trial court or a Court of Appeal in the United States and that a matter of constitutional law arises the constitutional matter is referred to the U.S. Supreme Court which gives its ruling on that particular matter, brings it back to the trial court and on the basis of recommendations from the U.S. Supreme Court, the appropriate judgment is passed.
The same principle, with a few variations, exists in Yugoslavia, Germany, France and countries of the European Economic Community. Perhaps we have there a striking example of a court strictly specialized in the interpretation of the respective jurisdictions of the various European Community member states and which has no other competence. That is then complete, total specialization in constitutional matters. That is what Canada is lacking.
That constitutional court that we could establish through a reform in depth of our present Supreme Court versus general competence in appeals, could have exclusive and first jurisdiction in disputes occurring between provinces and the federal government, or still between provinces, or in the interpretation of the constitutionality of a federal or provincial law. It would be its sole and exclusive competence.
I suggest decisions would then receive much better acceptance among the parties involved, and we would indeed have a worthy adjudicating body, an impartial one, to the extent of course provinces would have their say in the selection of members of the court. This could therefore be a part of an organization that could render highly specialized decisions in constitutional areas. Maybe we could use the suggestion by the hon. member for Central
Supreme Court Act
Nova (Mr. MacKay) that citizens should be given an opportunity to refer to that court points of law, for adjudication, without having to go through the usual process of superior court, appellant court and all the way to the Supreme Court, if and when the latter accept to hear the case. I believe this cannot be done under the current Supreme Court Act. If reform were undertaken to establish a body with exclusive specialized jurisdiction in the constitutional field, this would be possible.
Madam Speaker, I will conclude these brief remarks by commending the hon. member for Central Nova for raising the matter. Once more, this is a most interesting constitutional problem, and I very much hope we can achieve the objective he pointed out, in the years to come or at least during a subsequent federal-provincial conference.

speechtext:
Speak up, Marcel, so that Hansard can hear you.
When I initially looked at this bill I had certain reservations about it. I thought it might open the door for the proliferation of constitutional wrangles. But, I see the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has fully covered this concern in the second proposed section which allows the court to decide if a question is "an important question". Deciding such questions has, of course, been the traditional role of our supreme courts. Therefore that apprehended shortcoming has been removed from the bill.
I congratulate the hon. member for Central Nova for bringing forward a bill which will, if passed, do something that is long overdue in this country, something toward which our jurisprudence is slowly edging. It will make our courts more accessible to citizens who have suffered a wrong or who wish to have their rights determined. These rights to access long ago were enshrined in the constitution of the United States. We are slowly moving in that direction.
It has always been a principle of our law that, when there is a wrong, our legal system must provide the remedy. That remedy should not have to come from our legislatures. It should be provided, bascially, by the courts. I support this bill as it is another progressive attempt to allow the courts to deal with private wrongs, so that private wrongs may be redressed by the existing legal system.
A similar principle should apply to the redress of minor wrongs. For example, individual purchasers of automobiles may encounter, individually, a minor amount of difficulty but, in the mass, there may be losses of millions and millions of dollars. I am referring, of course, to class action legislation under which classes of persons in this country would be empowered to go to court, or send a representative to court, in order to redress what is basically a private wrong multiplied thousands and thousands of times. If we would come forward with that kind of legislation we would provide deterrents to some of the sloppy manufacturers in this country who are not faced with the same kind of legal risk as their counterparts in the United

July 18, 1975
Supreme Court Act
States. I suggest that would be a forward move in terms of Canadian legislation.
The same is true in the area where we have environmental laws. However, the amount of damage that any individual may suffer is so slight that, without status in a court for an individual, there is no deterrent to the industry that is doing the polluting. If we provide status to the entire group that has suffered the wrong, then the courts can provide some remedy.
I again congratulate the hon. member for what is really another process of democratization in the courts to see that individual rights are protected. The hon. member emphasized the problem of the power of the state. We in our western societies all have some concern that the power of the state is increasing. However, he did not mention the power of the corporate section of the community which is increasing at an even faster rate than that of the state. None of these things are good.
We all agree that the unlimited power of the state needs control. However, at the moment the power of bigness of corporations and, yes, trade unions has to be looked at in terms of protection against private wrongs that can result out of the idiom personality of these large organizations.
The hon. member for Lafontaine (Mr. Lachance) indicated that he did not believe the Supreme Court of Canada was a constitutional court although for a long time we have had the Constitutional Questions Determination Act. That court has been ruling on questions of the constitution and it has been doing a good job. I do not think we should have a separate court. The unique makeup of Canada in a federal state makes it imperative that we have a federal court by which all of the component parts, the provinces and otherwise, are bound. Certainly if there is a weakness in that, I would support a change.
In the circumstances I want to make these remarks as brief as I can. I congratulate the hon. member on the bill. It is a progressive step to give an individual the right to determine a constitutional matter affecting him.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is significant that this bill is brought on at this time by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) when the Supreme Court of Canada is this year celebrating its one hundredth anniversary.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CONFER CONSTITUTIONAL REFERENCE RIGHTS ON CITIZENS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CONFER CONSTITUTIONAL REFERENCE RIGHTS ON CITIZENS
speechtext:
We in this land are very blessed to have such a high quality of court. It has been so, and improvingly so since confederation. This court has consistently grown with the needs of our community with the administration of justice. It has continued to be as it should be, an independent branch of our parliamentary and democratic system, separate from the legislative branch and the executive branch. They have been an outstanding court. They continue to be so under the leadership of the most eminent Chief Justice of the Supreme Court who holds that position at the present time.
On the occasion of the celebration of the one hundredth anniversary of the court this fall, there will be very distinguished visitors coming to Canada, including the Lord

High Chancellor of Great Britain, le premier president de la Cour des Sessions de France, and Mr. Justice Byron White of the Supreme Court of the United States. I am sure we who are here join with the members of that court in wishing them a great celebration upon this occasion.
May I say to the hon. member for Central Nova that although at first blush his bill seems to indicate that he is entering upon a new field, in fact this is the type of field in which the Supreme Court has been entertaining applications and granting leave to appeal.
There was one case from the hon. member's province which was decided recently. It was a very important case, the Nova Scotia Board of Censors versus Gerald McNeil. The case had to do with the constitutionality and whether or not it was ultra vires of the province to pass a certain law. This one individual as a taxpayer and citizen was granted the right by the Supreme Court of Canada to have his appeal heard, and it was heard. Therefore, I cannot agree with the bill in its present form for some reasons, one of which was referred to by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt).
The hon. member said he was concerned about the bill in the first instance but he thought that subclause (2) would eliminate the dockets of the Supreme Court being overly cluttered by frivolous and vexatious matters-those were not his words-but so many matters of a constitutional nature. He said that subclause (2) granted to the court the right to determine what question it would or would not hear. I would point out that although perhaps the Supreme Court does have this right to determine what in their view are matters of importance and what they will hear, it would result in many hundreds of applications for leave to appeal the very items that the hon. member for Central Nova raises in his bill.
The practical part is that the applications for leave to appeal can and very often are an argument on the substance of the matter as well as an application to ask the court if they will hear it. Therefore it would take a tremendous amount of time, in any case involving a substantial issue, for the court just to deal with the applications for leave to appeal.
The proposals contained in this bill are unnecessary and are possessed of possibly very unfortunate consequences. Why this is so may be examined in terms of the two fundamental thrusts of the bill, namely, the standing of persons to launch the proceedings sought to be authorized by the bill and the nature of those proceedings that are to be in the form of a reference.
I will first address myself to standing. The bill assumes that the present laws relating to the standing of persons to bring before the courts "an important question of law or fact concerning the constitution of Canada or any public general law made by or under the authority of the parliament of Canada" are inadequate.
In two recent Supreme Court of Canada decisions, one of which I referred to earlier, the first being Thorson versus Attorney General of Canada, a general member of the taxpaying public was given standing to question the validity of the Official Languages Act, and the Nova Scotia Board of Censors versus McNeil, where a member of the public was permitted to attack the constitutional
July 18, 1975

validity of the provincial Theatres and Amusements Act, the highest court in the land acknowledged that it is not unlikely that the discretion of the court may be exercised in favour of giving standing to the sort of persons contemplated by this bill to question the constitutional validity of federal or provincial enactments.
In the first case, Thorson versus Attorney General of Canada, the former president of the Exchequer Court of Canada appeared personally to argue the case. He is acknowledged by all those who know him to be an exceptional man, an exceptional jurist, and an exceptional member of the bar. He argued this case as an individual without the necessity of Bill C-239 or any such legislation.
As a citizen and taxpayer, he argued as forcibly as he could to the Supreme Court that he had a right to be heard by the Supreme Court because it not only affected him as an individual but many other taxpayers. He argued that he should be permitted to be heard by the highest court in this land. He was heard, and he was given a full hearing. The Supreme Court of Canada recognized that this man, who was appearing not as a former jurist, not as the former president of the Exchequer Court of Canada, but as an individual, had the right on an important constitutional issue to be given a full hearing. I say this to indicate only that where there is such a matter of pressing and obvious concern the Supreme Court of Canada has grown and will continue to grow with the needs of the country as they relate to the administration of justice.
This liberal view of the standing of private citizens to bring into issue the constitutional validity of legislation was based in part, in the Thorson case, on Canadian and English jurisprudence dealing with standing in relation to the exercise of non-legislative powers and, in particular, on the powerful case of Dyson v. Attorney General decided by the English Court of Appeal more than 60 years ago. In terms of the respective legislative powers of parliament and the provincial legislatures, this is not a basis which may be strictly described as constitutional, and therefore it may be too early to say how far Canadian courts will be willing to take the laws of standing in non-constitutional situations. In view of these developments it may well be that the bill is not necessary to accomplish its stated purpose.
Even if the courts were not prepared to grant standing in a particular case, such as the case to which I have referred involving the former Mr. Justice Thorson and the case of the Nova Scotia Board of Censors and Gerald McNeil, the general law of the land already provides that an important question, to use the language of the bill, may in theory at least be litigated in non-reference proceedings by the appropriate Attorney General acting as parens patriae. Of course, it is where an Attorney General has been reluctant to do so that private persons have acted and, as in the two cases decided by the Supreme Court,- the cases to which I have referred-have been permitted to proceed. Moreover, there remains in the governor in council the authority under the Supreme Court Act to have important questions referred to the court for an advisory opinion.
Supreme Court Act
These provisions in the Supreme Court Act to which I have referred are section 55 in particular and section 35. First of all, may I refer to the general jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada as contained in section 35 of the Supreme Court Act:
The Supreme Court shall have, hold and exercise an appellate civil and criminal jurisdiction within and throughout Canada.
Section 36 states:
Subject to sections 40 and 44 an appeal to the Supreme Court lies from a final judgment or a judgment granting a motion for a non-suit or directing a new trial of the highest court of final resort in a province or a judge thereof, pronounced in
(a) a judicial proceeding where the amount or value of the matter in
controversy in the appeal exceeds $10,000, or the proceedings upon a
writ of habeus corpus.
Or two other matters. Therefore, Madam Speaker, the general power as set out in sections 35 and 36 is that the Supreme Court has the ultimate authority in this nation with respect to all criminal and civil matters subject to a monetary amount.
If the Supreme Court of Canada were to entertain cases of a similar nature involving $500 or $1,000 there would be so many cases before the court that it would have a difficult time directing itself to setting the precedents upon which the country relies so much for the administration of justice.
I, personally, over here on my side, have great respect for and great confidence in the judges of the provincial courts, both the civil and criminal divisions. I also have great respect for and confidence in the County Court and District Court judges who are appointed by the Canadian Governor General in Council, and also for the Supreme Courts of the provinces and the courts of appeal of the provinces which each have within their terms of reference limits within which they exercise final authority.
To say that the Supreme Court of the province of Ontario or the Court of Appeal of the province of Ontario is not able satisfactorily to answer all questions when we have set a monetary limit, for example, of $5,000 is, to my mind, to undermine the authority of those courts which have continued to demonstrate excellence in their judgments, whether they be appointments of provincial governments or whether they are appointed by the federal government.
I have great faith. I think the manner in which we have set out their jurisdiction, through acts of this parliament or acts of provincial legislatures, should not be lightly tampered with; it should be altered only when there is a pressing need to do so, and I do not find such a pressing need, especially in view of what has been demonstrated as being the actions of the Supreme Court of Canada in the two very recent cases I have quoted.
I should like to pay a little special attention to the intervention of one of my learned friends, the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemount (Mr. Lachance). At the beginning of my remarks I drew attention to the one hundredth anniversary of the Supreme Court of Canada. He has just celebrated, I think, the 21st anniversary of his birth, not very long ago. He demonstrated by the content of his speech today that he is a learned man. He arrived in this House with a bachelor's degree in arts, I believe; he
