speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CONFER CONSTITUTIONAL REFERENCE RIGHTS ON CITIZENS
speechtext:
If I could quickly summarize what I have been saying, it is that to give any person the right to refer such questions to the court might be harmful and unfortunate for the following reasons: (a) the distinction between frivolous or vexatious questions and those which deserve serious considerations might be lost; (b) The court would lose control of its docket which might become so filled with these private references that ordinary, and perhaps much more important appeal, would be subject to lengthy delays; (c) the avowed purpose of the amendments to the Supreme Court Act abolishing appeals as of right in civil matters, to lessen the already heavy case load of the court, would be defeated in part.
Further, even requiring the court first to determine whether a question is an important question would place an onerous burden on the court because (i) it would increase the list of motions for leave to appeal, and (ii) there would not necessarily be any record or other basis present on which the court could make a reasoned decision on this question. This procedure is contrary to the general principle that only the governor in council in the case of the Supreme Court, and the lieutenant governors in council in the case of the provincial courts, should be able to refer hypothetical cases to the court for advisory opinions. Because of the costs involved in the litigation process, this procedure would favour those individuals and corporations in Canada with the necessary means to bear those costs, and allowing other interested persons to be represented fails to deal with this matter of economics and with a procedure that favours issues by those financially capable of paying for such a reference.
I conclude my remarks by saying that I believe the Supreme Court of Canada has amply demonstrated its ability to exercise its discretion in granting the right of appeal on constitutional matters to individuals in this country in a most exemplary manner in both the Thorson case and the McNeil case to which I have referred. Therefore I submit there is no need or necessity for Bill C-239, though I compliment the hon. member for Central Nova for bringing it on for discussion.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CONFER CONSTITUTIONAL REFERENCE RIGHTS ON CITIZENS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, surely the hon. member's purpose for introducing this bill is highly commendable. He wants all Canadians to be enlightened concerning the constitutional significance of parliamentary legislation. In spite of his commendable purpose, however, I suggest that accepting such an amendment would mean accepting the Supreme Court of Canada as the indisputable authority with regard to the Canadian constitution.
Madam Speaker, if we were to accept such an amendment, there would be a general outcry in the province of Quebec.
Personally, I should be one of the first to denounce it, because a lot of Quebecers do not trust the Supreme Court, and they have a great many reasons not to do so. So I do not think we are ready yet to accept the authority of the
Supreme Court in constitutional matters. I am therefore almost in agreement with the hon. member for Lafon-taine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) when he says that only a body which would really represent the constituent elements of our country in a fair and equitable fashion would have this sort of authority which the Supreme Court would need to really render decisions in cases of conflicts. As a matter of fact, we are faced with one of these issues in the area of cablevision, and, Madam Speaker, when I heard the Prime Minister state in reply to my question that the federal government would not budge from its position, I was perfectly aware that a great many jurists could come forward and argue that under our constitution, communications, radio, television and cable television fall indeed under provincial jurisdiction. Then, at a given time, someone will have to decide where other agreements will be necessary, but in any case I am not sure that the opinion of the Supreme Court is undoubtedly the best because the Supreme Court is a creature of the federal government. It is always a little difficult in this very badly made country to make a judgment on these things because a country which, by virtue of its constitution, is a confederation is not a confederation after all. It is not a group of states which are in agreement, which unite for the best and for the worse, but it rather is a federation.
Yet, there is something ambiguous in our country which prevents us from being able to refer to a real constitutional authority, for the simple reason that there is no such authority: the Supreme Court is a creature and an organization of the federal government. Theoretically, it could therefore stand up for Parliament which it is a creature of and responsible to. And to those who claim that there is a host of extremely contentious issues on that matter, I would give as an example the matter of cablevision which is presently under discussion. However, one must admit that in spite of all these remarks that would obviously cause me to oppose such a bill, one must admit nevertheless that it should be good, Madam Speaker, to know just when the legislation passed by the Parliament of Canada is within the terms of the constitution. That would in effect avoid a number of problems which we meet and have met. And, if the Supreme Court were truly the body needed to solve all the problems, one would never have seen Madam Speaker, the frightful injustices that French-Canadians, or Quebecers have suffered which have never been redressed since provinces have made rules to abolish the French language. They have passed rules that could be judged as anticonstitutional. There was no authority to settle this problem, and even the federal Parliament's position on this matter is difficult to admit for some provinces. Then, it remains that the organization needed to make a decision should issue from every provincial authority so that we could refer to it if needed. But it would be very difficult now to refer to an organization that could stand up for one of the parties. This is why, despite the very commendable object of the bill, I would be inclined to reject it as long as the situation remains unchanged. May I say it is five o'clock?
